q:
Overnight Oats (makes 2 servings)
1 cup rolled oats
1 cup milk
½ cup plain yogurt
1 tablespoon honey
½ cup berries

Directions: Mix all ingredients except the berries in a jar. Refrigerate for at least 6 hours. Top with the berries just before serving. A student wants to make 4 servings. How much milk will she need?
e: The recipe makes 2 servings, so 4 servings means doubling everything.
1 cup × 2 = 2 cups. 4 cups is the trap of using one cup per serving.

q:
Overnight Oats (makes 2 servings)
1 cup rolled oats
1 cup milk
½ cup plain yogurt
1 tablespoon honey
½ cup berries

Directions: Mix all ingredients except the berries in a jar. Refrigerate for at least 6 hours. Top with the berries just before serving. According to the recipe, when should the berries be added?
o: While mixing the oats and milk
e: The directions say to mix everything EXCEPT the berries and to top with them "just before serving."

q:
A pamphlet about type 2 diabetes has the following headings:
I. What Is Type 2 Diabetes?
II. Who Is at Risk?
III. ______
IV. How Is Type 2 Diabetes Treated? Which heading best fits in the blank?
e: The headings move logically from what the disease is, to who gets it, to finding it, to treating it.
Diagnosis fits between risk and treatment. The other headings are off topic or out of place in this sequence.

q:
Drug Facts
Active ingredient (in each tablet)Ibuprofen 200 mg
Usestemporarily relieves minor aches and pains, headache, and toothache; temporarily reduces fever
Directions: adults and children 12 years and oldertake 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours while symptoms last. If pain or fever does not respond to 1 tablet, 2 tablets may be used. Do not take more than 6 tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor.
Children under 12 yearsask a doctor
Which statements are supported by the label? Select all that apply.
o: An adult may take 2 tablets at once if 1 tablet does not help.
An adult may take up to 6 tablets in 24 hours without asking a doctor.
A 10-year-old should take 1 tablet every 6 hours.
The medicine can be used to lower a fever.
An adult may take 1 tablet every 2 hours.
e: The label allows 2 tablets if 1 does not work, a maximum of 6 in 24 hours, and lists "reduces fever" under Uses.
Children under 12 should "ask a doctor," so no dose is given for a 10-year-old.
Doses are every 4 to 6 hours, not every 2 hours.

q: The guide words at the top of a dictionary page are lumbar and lymph. Which word would appear on this page?
e: Words on the page fall alphabetically between the two guide words.
"lung" (l-u-n) comes after "lumbar" (l-u-m) and before "lymph" (l-y).
"lucid" (l-u-c) and "lumbago" (l-u-m-b-a-g, and g comes before r) come before "lumbar"; "lymphoma" comes after "lymph."
t: Compare guide words letter by letter until the first letter that differs.

q:
Children in the United States usually receive the MMR vaccine in two doses. The first dose is given at 12 to 15 months of age, and the second at 4 to 6 years. The vaccine protects against three diseases: measles, mumps, and rubella.

What is the author's main purpose?
o: To persuade parents to refuse the MMR vaccine
To inform readers about when children receive the MMR vaccine
To entertain readers with a story about a child's checkup
To express the author's fear of measles
e: The passage gives facts (doses, ages, diseases) without opinions or a story, so its purpose is to inform.
It does not argue against vaccines, tell a story, or share feelings.
t: Purpose shortcut: Inform = facts, Persuade = opinion + call to act, Entertain = story or humor, Express = feelings.

q:
Every student on this campus deserves a quiet place to study between classes. The library closes at 6 p.m., yet many of us work during the day and take evening classes. I urge the student senate to keep at least one floor of the library open until 10 p.m.

What is the author's primary purpose?
o: To persuade the student senate to extend library hours
To inform readers about the history of the library
To describe the evening classes offered on campus
To entertain readers with a story about studying
e: "I urge the student senate" is a call to action, which signals a persuasive purpose.
The passage gives no library history, does not describe classes, and tells no story.

q:
On my first day as a hospital volunteer, I proudly pushed a patient's wheelchair down the hall and straight into the supply closet. The patient laughed so hard that she asked me to do it again on the way back.

What is the author's main purpose?
o: To teach readers how to push a wheelchair safely
To persuade students to volunteer at hospitals
To inform readers about the layout of a hospital
To entertain readers with a funny story
e: The passage is a short, humorous personal story, and its goal is to amuse.
It gives no instructions, makes no argument, and does not describe the hospital's layout.

q:
You will probably feel nervous before your first clinical rotation. Your hands may shake as you take your first blood pressure. Remember that your instructor expects you to be learning, not to be perfect.

From which point of view is the passage written?
e: The author speaks directly to the reader using "you" and "your," which is second person.
First person would use "I" or "we"; third person would use "he," "she," or "they."

q:
Some people say the planned freeway expansion will cut commute times. Perhaps it will. But the plan would also bulldoze forty homes in one of Fresno's oldest neighborhoods and bring more truck exhaust near two elementary schools. Faster commutes are a poor trade for families' homes and children's lungs.

Which statement best describes the author's point of view?
o: The author supports the freeway expansion.
The author has no opinion about the freeway expansion.
The author opposes the freeway expansion.
The author is mainly concerned about commute times.
e: The author admits the expansion might shorten commutes, then argues that the costs to homes and health are too high.
The last sentence, "a poor trade," clearly shows opposition.

q:
(1) Most people think of bones as dry, lifeless sticks. (2) In fact, bone is living tissue that constantly breaks down and rebuilds itself. (3) Cells called osteoclasts dissolve old bone, while osteoblasts lay down new bone. (4) This ongoing process is what allows a broken bone to heal.

Why does the author most likely include sentence 1?
o: To introduce a common belief that the passage will correct
To explain how osteoclasts dissolve old bone tissue
To persuade readers to drink more milk for strong bones
To state the main idea that the rest of the passage supports
e: Sentence 1 states a common idea, and "In fact" in sentence 2 corrects it.
The main idea, that bone is living tissue, is in sentence 2, not sentence 1. Osteoclasts are explained in sentence 3, and milk is never mentioned.

q:
It is shameful that, in one of the richest farming regions on Earth, many of the families who harvest our food still struggle to afford groceries. We should not accept this.

Which word best describes the author's tone?
e: Words like "shameful" and "We should not accept this" show anger at an unfair situation, which is an indignant tone.
Nothing is funny, the language is not neutral, and the author expresses outrage rather than hope.

q: An author writes a brochure for a dialysis center that explains what new patients can expect at their first appointment. What is the author's primary purpose?
o: To persuade patients to switch centers
e: Explaining what to expect gives readers information, so the purpose is to inform.
A brochure for the same center would not urge patients to go elsewhere.

q:
Telehealth visits saved many patients a long drive during the pandemic, and for routine follow-ups they remain a sensible choice. But a video screen cannot replace a nurse's hands. A swollen ankle, a faint rash, or the smell of an infected wound can be missed when a patient is seen only through a camera.

Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
o: Telehealth visits should no longer be offered to patients.
Video visits are better than office visits for spotting rashes and swelling.
Telehealth is useful for some visits but should not replace all in-person exams.
Most patients would rather drive long distances than use telehealth for visits.
e: The author calls telehealth "sensible" for routine follow-ups but warns about what it can miss.
The author does not want to end telehealth, says video visits can MISS rashes, and never says patients prefer long drives.

q:
The waiting room was crowded, and Mrs. Flores clutched her purse. She had not seen a doctor in five years, and she wondered whether the nurse would scold her. When the nurse smiled and said, "I'm so glad you came in," Mrs. Flores felt her shoulders relax.

From whose point of view is the passage told?
o: Mrs. Flores herself, describing her visit in the first person
A third-person narrator who shares Mrs. Flores's thoughts
The nurse, describing Mrs. Flores in the first person
A narrator who speaks directly to the reader, using "you" throughout
e: The narrator uses "she" and "her" (third person) and tells us what Mrs. Flores wonders and feels.
There is no "I" narrator, and the reader is never addressed as "you." The nurse's words are quoted, but the story is not told by the nurse.

q: An article about heat illness begins with a short story about a young farmworker who collapsed in a vineyard on a 108 °F afternoon. What is the most likely reason the author begins this way?
o: To prove that every farmworker will develop heat illness
To entertain readers with a humorous anecdote
To give statistics about how often heat illness occurs in California
To capture readers' interest and show the real danger of the topic
e: Opening with a real-life-style story is a common way to hook readers and make a danger feel personal.
One story cannot prove what happens to EVERY worker, the story is not funny, and a story is not a statistic.
t: Opening anecdotes are usually there to hook the reader.

q:
A visit to an urgent care center for a minor sprain usually costs a fraction of what the same care costs in an emergency room, and the wait is often much shorter. For problems that are not life-threatening, urgent care is often the better choice. Chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke, however, always call for the ER.

What is the author's main purpose?
o: To persuade readers never to visit the emergency room
To complain about long waits in emergency rooms
To explain how emergency rooms and urgent care centers are paid for
To help readers decide when to use urgent care instead of the ER
e: The author compares the two options and tells readers which situations fit each one.
The author says some problems ALWAYS need the ER, so "never" is wrong. Waits are mentioned as a reason, not as a complaint, and funding is not discussed.

q:
My grandmother's hands were rough from forty summers in the vineyards near Selma, but they were the gentlest hands I have ever known. Whenever I was sick, she would rest one cool palm on my forehead and hum until I fell asleep.

What is the author's main purpose?
o: To inform readers about the grape harvest near Selma
To express love and admiration for her grandmother
To persuade readers to care for sick children at home
To explain how to treat rough, dry skin
e: The warm memories and words like "gentlest" show that the author is sharing feelings.
The vineyards are background, and the passage gives no facts about harvests, no argument, and no skin-care advice.

q: A pamphlet praising a new sports drink was written and paid for by the company that makes the drink. What is most likely the pamphlet's main purpose?
o: To compare the drink fairly with water
To persuade readers to buy the drink
To express the writer's personal feelings
e: A company writing about its own product usually wants readers to buy it.
A seller's pamphlet that "praises" the product is not a fair comparison.

q:
Should nursing students be allowed to use their phones during clinical rotations? A drug-reference app can answer a question about a medication in seconds. Yet a student glancing at a screen might miss a change in a patient's color or breathing. On balance, the answer seems to be yes, but only for reference apps, and only away from the bedside.

Which statement best describes the author's point of view?
o: The author supports limited phone use during clinicals.
The author is completely against phone use during clinicals.
The author supports unlimited phone use during clinicals.
The author does not take a position on phone use.
e: The author weighs a benefit and a risk, then concludes "yes, but only" in certain conditions.
That is a limited yes: not a full ban, not unlimited use, and not neutral.
t: Read the last sentence carefully; authors often state their position there.

q:
Energy drinks are marketed as a harmless boost for tired students, but the reality is far less cheerful. A single can may contain as much caffeine as three cups of coffee, plus a staggering amount of sugar. Students who reach for these sugary jolts night after night may end up jittery, sleepless, and no better prepared for their exams.

Which phrases from the passage show the author's negative attitude toward energy drinks? Select all that apply.
e: "Far less cheerful," "staggering," and "sugary jolts" are word choices that make energy drinks sound bad.
"Tired students" describes the buyers, and "three cups of coffee" is a neutral comparison of caffeine amounts.

q: Which of the following was most likely written mainly to entertain?
o: A chart comparing average starting pay for nurses in five California cities
A letter urging county voters to approve a bond measure for a new children's hospital
A short story about a nursing student who adopts a goat during finals week
A brochure listing a community clinic's hours, services, and accepted insurance plans
e: A funny short story is written to entertain.
A pay chart and a clinic brochure inform, and a letter urging voters persuades.

q:
Valley fever cases in California have risen sharply over the past decade. Scientists link the increase to cycles of drought followed by heavy rain, which help the fungus grow in the soil and then spread in dust.

That is why the county must pay for a public awareness campaign now. Too many residents mistake valley fever for the flu and go months without a correct diagnosis.

How does the author's purpose change from the first paragraph to the second?
o: It shifts from entertaining readers to informing them about the fungus.
It shifts from persuading readers to informing them about the flu and its symptoms.
It shifts from describing valley fever symptoms to telling a personal story.
It shifts from informing readers about rising cases to urging the county to act.
e: Paragraph 1 gives facts about the increase and its causes, which is informative.
Paragraph 2 says the county "must" pay for a campaign, which is persuasive.

q: In an editorial calling for a new crosswalk near a high school, the author writes, "Twelve pedestrians have been struck at this intersection in the past three years." Why does the author most likely include this statistic?
o: To show that the intersection is dangerous and needs a crosswalk
To show that drivers near the school are usually careful
To inform readers about the history of the high school
To entertain readers with a surprising fact
e: A persuasive writer uses numbers as evidence. Twelve people struck shows the danger and supports the call for a crosswalk.
The statistic suggests the opposite of careful drivers, and it has nothing to do with the school's history or entertainment.

q:
At last, families in Huron won't have to drive an hour to see a doctor. The new clinic, opening in May, is a long-overdue victory for our community.

Which word best describes the author's attitude toward the new clinic?
e: "At last" and "a long-overdue victory" show that the author is excited and pleased.
Skeptical means doubtful, indifferent means not caring, and disappointed means let down; none of these fit.

q: The nurse noticed that the patient was lethargic; he could barely keep his eyes open, and he answered questions slowly. Based on the context, what does lethargic mean?
e: The clues "could barely keep his eyes open" and "answered questions slowly" describe someone sluggish and drowsy.
Restless and talkative are close to the opposite, and nothing in the sentence mentions fever.
t: Replace the word with each choice. The right one keeps the sentence's meaning.

q:
Because the mountains around the San Joaquin Valley trap air like the sides of a bowl, pollution from cars, trucks, and farms builds up over cities such as Fresno and Bakersfield. As a result, the region has some of the worst air quality in the nation, and children here have higher rates of asthma.

Which best describes how the passage is organized?
e: Signal words "Because" and "As a result" link a cause (trapped air) to effects (poor air, more asthma).
Nothing is compared, no timeline is given, and no solution is offered.

q:
Both type 1 and type 2 diabetes cause high blood sugar. In type 1, the body makes little or no insulin, so patients must take insulin every day. In type 2, the body makes insulin but does not use it well, and many patients can manage the disease at first with diet, exercise, and pills.

Which best describes how the passage is organized?
e: "Both" shows a similarity, and the descriptions of type 1 versus type 2 show differences.
Showing how two things are alike and different is compare and contrast.

q: A nurse wants to describe, in a positive way, a patient who asks many questions about his treatment. Which word should she choose?
e: "Curious" has a positive connotation: interested and eager to learn.
"Nosy," "pushy," and "demanding" all carry negative feelings.

q: The nurse asked the patient to rate his pain on a scale of 0 to 10. In which sentence is the word scale used with the same meaning as in the sentence above?
o: The nurse carefully weighed the newborn on the scale in the nursery.
On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied were you with your visit?
The hikers had to scale the steep granite wall.
The fish's silver scales shone in the bright afternoon sunlight.
e: In the original sentence, a scale is a range of numbers used to rate something.
The other sentences use different meanings: a weighing device, to climb, and the plates on a fish's skin.

q:
Many patients forget to take their medicines on time. To help, some pharmacies now offer blister packs labeled with the day and time of each dose, and others send text-message reminders.

Which best describes how the passage is organized?
e: The first sentence states a problem (forgetting doses), and the second gives ways to solve it.

q: Unlike her gregarious roommate, who loved crowded parties, Lily preferred quiet evenings alone. What does gregarious most likely mean?
e: "Unlike" signals a contrast: Lily likes quiet evenings, so her roommate is the opposite.
Someone who loves crowded parties is sociable and outgoing. "Shy and quiet" describes Lily, not the roommate.
t: Words like unlike, but, and however signal an antonym clue.

q: The cut on the child's knee was superficial, so the nurse simply cleaned it and applied a bandage; no stitches were needed. As used in the sentence, what does superficial mean?
e: Because the cut needed only cleaning and a bandage, not stitches, it was shallow.
Superficial (super- = above, -ficial from "face" or surface) means on the surface.

q:
In 1918, influenza spread across the world in three waves. The first, in the spring, was fairly mild. The second, which arrived in the fall, was far deadlier and killed many healthy young adults. By the summer of 1919, the third wave had faded.

Which best describes how the passage is organized?
e: The passage moves through time (1918 spring, fall, then 1919 summer) to describe the three waves in order.

q: Two newspapers described the same speech by a city council member. One said she explained her housing plan to the audience. The other said she lectured the audience about her plan. How does the word lectured change the meaning?
o: It suggests she spoke clearly and helpfully to the audience.
It suggests she was preachy and talked down to the audience.
It suggests that she works as a teacher at a local college.
It suggests that the audience agreed with every part of her plan.
e: "Explained" is neutral, but "lectured" has a negative connotation of scolding or talking down to people.
It does not mean she is a teacher, and it hints the audience may NOT have liked it.

q: Many older adults take several prescription medicines at the same time, a situation known as polypharmacy. Based on the sentence, what does polypharmacy mean?
e: The sentence defines the term directly: polypharmacy is the situation of taking several medicines at the same time.
The root poly- means "many," which also points to the answer.

q:
After a 12-hour shift, Rosa's feet were blocks of lead.

What does the author mean?
o: Rosa was wearing heavy work boots.
Rosa's feet felt very heavy and tired.
Rosa had injured her feet at work.
e: This is a metaphor: lead is a heavy metal, so her feet FELT heavy after a long shift.
The sentence is figurative. Rosa's feet are not literally made of lead, and no injury or boots are mentioned.

q: Acute pain begins suddenly, after a cut, a burn, or surgery, and usually fades as the body heals. Chronic pain, by contrast, lasts for months or even years. As used in the passage, acute most nearly means
e: The passage defines acute pain as beginning suddenly and fading with healing, and contrasts it with long-lasting chronic pain.
"Sharp and intense" is another common meaning of acute, but it is not the meaning used here.
t: "As used in the passage" means the most common meaning may be a trap. Check the context.

q: The patient's compliance with her treatment plan was poor: she skipped doses, missed two appointments, and never started the walking program her doctor recommended. As used in the sentence, compliance means
e: The examples after the colon (skipped doses, missed appointments) describe NOT following the plan.
So compliance means following instructions or the plan as directed.

q: The western side of the San Joaquin Valley is arid. Rain is scarce, sometimes less than six inches a year, and without irrigation the land would support little more than dry grasses and scrub. Which phrases are context clues for the meaning of arid? Select all that apply.
e: Scarce rain, very little rainfall, and dry plants all point to the meaning of arid: very dry.
The location phrases tell WHERE, not what arid means.

q:
The patient's fever had not come down after two doses of acetaminophen. ______, the nurse notified the provider.

Which transition best fits the blank?
e: The nurse called the provider BECAUSE the fever did not come down, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.
"However" shows contrast, "For example" introduces an example, and "Similarly" shows a likeness.

q:
The landlord made the repairs only after months of stalling.

Which word in the sentence suggests that the writer disapproves of the landlord?
e: "Stalling" means delaying on purpose, which has a negative connotation.
The other words are neutral.

q: The doctor told Mr. Chen that his biopsy results were negative, and he smiled with relief. As used in the sentence, negative means
o: the result was a number less than zero
the test did not find the disease
e: In medicine, a negative test result means the condition being tested for was not found.
Mr. Chen's relief is a clue that the news was good, so "bad news" is the everyday-meaning trap.

q: Put these sentences in the most logical order to form a paragraph.
o: A vaccine introduces a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ into the body.
The immune system responds by making antibodies and memory cells.
Later, if the real germ enters the body, the memory cells recognize it.
The body then fights off the germ quickly, often before the person feels sick.
e: The paragraph follows a cause-and-effect chain: the vaccine goes in, the body responds, the memory cells recognize the real germ later, and the body fights it off.
Words like "responds," "Later," and "then" help show the order.

q: Which pair of words has nearly the same denotation but different connotations?
e: Thrifty and cheap both mean careful with money, but "thrifty" sounds positive and "cheap" sounds negative.
Doctor and physician share both meaning and neutral feeling; hot/cold are opposites; nurse/patient are different people.
t: Denotation = dictionary meaning. Connotation = the feeling a word carries.

q: Which statement is an opinion?
o: The new hospital wing has 120 patient beds and four operating rooms.
The new hospital wing is the most beautiful building in Visalia.
The new hospital wing opened in March.
The new hospital wing has a helicopter pad on its roof for emergencies.
e: "Most beautiful" is a personal judgment that people could disagree about.
The number of beds, the opening date, and the helicopter pad can all be checked.
t: A fact can be checked. An opinion is a belief, judgment, or feeling.

q: Which statement is a fact?
o: The human heart has four chambers.
Nursing is the most rewarding career a person can choose.
Everyone should get a flu shot every year.
e: The number of heart chambers can be verified in any anatomy textbook.
"Most rewarding" and "tastes terrible" are judgments, and "should" signals a recommendation, which is an opinion.

q:
(1) The city's new bike lanes opened in April. (2) Since then, the number of cyclists counted on Blackstone Avenue has doubled. (3) The bike lanes are the smartest investment the city has made in decades. (4) The project cost $2.1 million.

Which sentence states an opinion?
e: "The smartest investment" is a judgment that cannot be proven.
The opening date, the cyclist count, and the cost could all be checked in records.

q: An article praising a new weight-loss supplement was written by a doctor who is paid by the company that sells it. What should a careful reader conclude?
o: The article must be accurate because a doctor wrote it.
The article is a neutral, reliable source.
The article may be biased in favor of the supplement.
e: When an author earns money from a product, he has a reason to present it favorably, so the article may be biased.
Being a doctor does not remove a conflict of interest, and bias alone does not prove the product is dangerous.

q: Which statement is a stereotype?
o: Some teenage drivers take dangerous risks.
Drivers under 20 have higher crash rates than middle-aged drivers.
Many teens take a driver's education course.
e: A stereotype applies a fixed idea to EVERY member of a group, as in "All teenagers are careless."
"Some" and "many" are limited statements, and crash rates are data, not stereotypes.

q:
The council's reckless budget cuts will gut the city's only free clinic.

Which words in the sentence reveal the writer's bias? Select all that apply.
e: "Reckless" (careless and dangerous) and "gut" (destroy from the inside) are loaded words that show the writer's strong disapproval.
"Council's," "budget," and "clinic" are neutral nouns.

q: Which sentence states a fact that could be verified?
o: The clinic's staff are the kindest and most caring people in the entire county.
The clinic's annual report shows it served a record number of patients in 2025.
The clinic should receive more funding next year.
Patients probably prefer the clinic to the hospital because the waits are shorter.
e: A reader could check the annual report to confirm the number of patients served.
"Kindest" is a judgment, "should" is a recommendation, and "probably prefer" is a guess.

q: Studies show that people who eat breakfast tend to have more energy in the morning. Clearly, skipping breakfast is the worst habit a student can have. The author uses the word clearly mainly to
o: present an opinion as though it were an obvious fact
introduce a statistic from a study of student habits
name the source of the information about breakfast
signal a contrast with the idea in the first sentence
e: "Clearly" makes the claim sound certain, but "the worst habit a student can have" is an opinion that the study does not prove.
No statistic or source follows the word, and it does not signal contrast the way "however" would.
t: Words like clearly, obviously, and everyone knows can disguise an opinion as a fact.

q: A student is researching whether a new diabetes medicine is safe. Which source is likely to be the least biased?
o: A study by researchers who got no money from the drug's maker
A television commercial paid for by the company that makes the drug
A blog by a person who sells herbal remedies that compete with the drug
A press release from the company that makes and sells the new drug
e: Researchers with no financial ties to the drug have the least reason to favor or attack it.
The commercial and press release come from the maker, and the blogger profits from a competing product.

q: The statement "Sacramento is the capital of California" is
o: an opinion, because not everyone agrees
a fact only because it appears in textbooks
an opinion, because an expert said it
a fact, because it can be checked
e: A fact can be proven true with reliable sources, such as a map or a state government website.
Whether something is a fact does not depend on who says it or where it is printed.

q: Which statement would be the most difficult to prove?
o: At sea level, water boils at 100 °C.
The best way to relax is to listen to music.
The clinic opens at 8 a.m. on weekdays.
Merced is located in the San Joaquin Valley.
e: "The best way" is a judgment; people relax in different ways, so it cannot be proven.
The boiling point, clinic hours, and location can all be checked.

q:
A brochure for Sunny Meadows Assisted Living highlights its rose garden, weekly outings, and chef-prepared meals. It does not mention the facility's staffing levels or the results of its most recent state inspection.

What can a careful reader conclude?
o: Sunny Meadows must have failed its most recent state inspection, or it would say so.
The brochure is an objective source of information about the facility.
The brochure shows only the positives, so the reader should check other sources.
Sunny Meadows does not have enough staff to care for all of its residents safely.
e: Leaving out important information is a form of bias; the brochure shows only the positives.
The missing information does not PROVE a failed inspection or low staffing; it means the reader should look elsewhere.

q:
Our town needs a dog park. (1) Dog owners here deserve better. (2) The nearest dog park is 14 miles away. (3) A dog park would make our town the friendliest in the valley. (4) Everyone loves dogs.

Which numbered sentence states a fact?
e: The distance to the nearest dog park can be measured.
"Deserve better," "the friendliest," and "Everyone loves dogs" are opinions or overgeneralizations.

q: Which word most often signals an opinion?
e: Superlatives like "best" usually express a judgment.
"Measured," "recorded," and "according to" point to evidence or sources.

q: A website that sells herbal tea states, "Doctors agree that our tea cures anxiety." What is the main problem with this claim?
o: It proves that herbal tea is dangerous for people with anxiety.
It is a fact, because doctors are the experts on health and anxiety.
It gives no named doctors or evidence, and it comes from the seller.
It is an opinion only because it is about a food rather than a medicine.
e: "Doctors agree" is vague: no doctors, studies, or numbers are given, and the seller profits from the claim.
The problem is lack of support, not proof of danger. Expert words still need evidence.

q: Which revision turns the opinion "The new urgent care center has terrible wait times" into a statement of fact?
o: The average wait at the new urgent care center last month was 74 minutes.
The new urgent care center has awful, frustrating wait times.
Everyone hates waiting so long at the new urgent care center down the street.
The new urgent care center should hire more staff.
e: A measured average wait time can be checked, so it is a fact.
"Awful" and "frustrating" are still judgments, "everyone hates" is an overgeneralization, and "should" is a recommendation.

q: A health blog states, "Drinking eight glasses of water a day is the only way to stay healthy." This statement is best described as
o: an opinion presented as a fact
a definition of a medical term
e: The statement sounds certain, but "the only way" is an exaggeration that cannot be proven.
No data are given, nothing is defined, and there are no steps.

q:
As a lifelong farmer, I can tell you that the proposed groundwater fees will destroy family farms across the valley. These fees are nothing more than a tax on the people who feed America.

Which best describes the author's bias?
o: The author strongly opposes the fees and writes as a farmer who would pay them.
The author supports the fees as a way to protect the valley's groundwater supply.
The author presents both sides of the groundwater issue fairly and equally.
The author is biased in favor of city residents who use less groundwater.
e: The author identifies as a farmer and uses strong words such as "destroy" and "nothing more than a tax."
Only one side is presented, and city residents are never mentioned.

q: Which statements are opinions? Select all that apply.
o: Nursing school is harder than medical school.
Night shifts are more interesting than day shifts.
The TEAS includes a reading section.
e: "Harder," "more interesting," and "should" express judgments that people may disagree with.
The number of counties and the sections of the TEAS can be checked.

q:
A survey found that 7 out of 10 patients rated the clinic "excellent." The clinic is therefore the best in the county.

Which part of the passage is a fact?
o: The claim that the clinic is the best in the county
The idea that every patient likes the clinic
The survey result about patient ratings
The idea that the clinic should expand
e: The survey result can be checked against the survey data.
"The best in the county" is an opinion that the survey does not prove. The last two choices are not in the passage.

q:
Our campus should offer free flu shots to all students. Last winter, flu outbreaks caused hundreds of missed classes, and many students could not afford to see a doctor.

What is the author's main claim?
o: Flu outbreaks caused hundreds of missed classes.
The campus should offer free flu shots to all students.
Many students could not afford to see a doctor.
Flu shots have serious side effects.
e: The claim is the position the author wants readers to accept: the campus should offer free flu shots.
Missed classes and doctor costs are evidence that support the claim. Side effects are never mentioned.
t: The claim is what the author wants you to believe; the evidence is the reason to believe it.

q: Which evidence best supports the claim that later school start times improve students' health?
o: Many students say they enjoy eating breakfast at home with their families before school.
Most teachers in one survey said they prefer an early start so they can leave school sooner in the afternoon.
School buses are expensive to operate, especially for districts that cover large rural areas.
After one district started school an hour later, students slept more and saw the school nurse less.
e: Only the district example connects a later start time with a health result (more sleep, fewer nurse visits).
The other choices are about breakfast habits, teacher preference, and cost, not student health.

q: A school claims that its new reading program raised third graders' test scores. Which fact, if true, would most weaken this claim?
o: Teachers in the school said they enjoyed using the new program.
The program cost the school about $10 per student each year to run.
Average scores rose by 12 points in the year after the program began.
The state made the test easier in the same year the program began.
e: If the test got easier, scores could have risen without any help from the program, so another explanation exists.
Teacher enjoyment and cost don't affect the claim, and a 12-point rise would support it.

q: "Dr. Gomez is an excellent heart surgeon, so her advice about which stocks to buy must be right." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
o: Surgeons are not allowed to give their patients advice of any kind.
Her skill in surgery does not make her an expert on investing.
The statement relies on too many statistics.
The statement attacks Dr. Gomez's character.
e: This is a false appeal to authority: expertise in one field is used to support a claim in an unrelated field.
The statement praises her, it does not attack her, and it contains no statistics.

q:
The county clinic should stay open on weekends. (1) Many patients work Monday through Friday and cannot come during the week. (2) The emergency room is crowded on weekends with patients who do not have emergencies. (3) The clinic building was painted blue last year. (4) During a trial, weekend appointments filled within hours.

Which sentence is NOT relevant to the argument?
e: The color of the building has nothing to do with whether weekend hours are needed.
Patients' work schedules, ER crowding, and fast-filling weekend appointments all support opening on weekends.

q: "My neighbor felt sick the day after his flu shot, so flu shots make people sick." What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
o: It relies on the opinion of a medical expert.
It attacks the character of people who get flu shots.
It draws a broad conclusion from a single example.
It offers only two choices when there are more.
e: One person's experience is not enough evidence for a claim about everyone. This is a hasty generalization.
No expert, personal attack, or either-or choice appears in the statement.

q:
Since the clinic began sending text-message reminders in January, patients have missed far fewer appointments. Therefore, the text reminders are what reduced missed appointments.

Which assumption does this argument depend on?
o: Nothing else changed at the same time that could explain the drop.
Patients dislike receiving text messages from the clinic.
The clinic also mails reminder cards to patients.
Most other clinics in the area do not send any appointment reminders.
e: The argument says the texts CAUSED the drop, which assumes there is no other explanation, such as a new bus route or easier scheduling.
Disliking texts would weaken the argument, mailed cards would be another explanation, and other clinics are irrelevant.
t: Ask: what else could explain the result? The argument assumes the answer is "nothing."

q:
According to a recent survey of 1,200 California nurses, 40 percent said they planned to leave their jobs within five years.

What type of evidence does the author use?
e: A survey result given as a percentage is statistical evidence.
An anecdote is a personal story, and an analogy compares two different things.

q: Claim: Planting shade trees in south Fresno neighborhoods would reduce heat-related illness. Which evidence would most strengthen this claim?
o: In a similar city, shadier blocks were up to 10 °F cooler and had fewer heat-related ER visits.
Trees provide shade and homes for many kinds of birds and insects in the city.
Some residents say they would prefer palm trees to oak trees on their streets.
Young trees must be watered often during hot summers, which can raise water bills for residents.
e: This evidence connects trees to both lower temperatures and fewer heat illnesses, which is exactly what the claim says.
Birds, tree preferences, and watering needs have nothing to do with heat illness.

q:
Some argue that limiting nurses to shifts of 12 hours or less would cause staffing shortages. However, research on fatigue shows that error rates rise sharply after 12 hours of work, and the cost of treating patients harmed by errors is far greater than the cost of hiring extra staff.

How does the author respond to the counterargument?
o: By agreeing that shift limits would cause too many staffing problems
By arguing that fatigue-related errors cost more than extra staff
By attacking the character of the people who disagree with the author
By changing the subject to how much nurses are paid for overtime
e: The author states the opposing view, then uses "However" to give evidence that errors are more costly than extra staff.
The author does not agree with the opposing side, does not insult anyone, and does not discuss pay.

q:
(1) Seat belts cut the risk of death in a crash nearly in half for front-seat passengers. (2) Yet some drivers skip buckling up on short trips. (3) Many crashes happen close to home. (4) Therefore, everyone should wear a seat belt on every trip, no matter how short.

Which sentence states the author's conclusion?
e: "Therefore" signals the conclusion, which is drawn from the facts in sentences 1–3.

q: "Either we close the hospital's maternity ward, or the entire hospital will go bankrupt." What is the main flaw in this statement?
o: It attacks the character of the people who disagree.
It relies on a single personal example.
It cites an expert from an unrelated field.
It presents only two choices when other options may exist.
e: This is a false dilemma (either-or reasoning): there may be other ways to save money, such as cutting other costs or finding grants.

q: Which piece of evidence is strongest for the claim that a new asthma inhaler reduces emergency room visits?
o: A patient who says that the new inhaler has completely changed her life for the better
A company website that calls the inhaler "clinically proven" and "doctor recommended"
A randomized study of 2,000 patients that found 30 percent fewer ER visits with the new inhaler
A doctor who says she likes prescribing the new inhaler to many of her patients with asthma
e: A large, randomized study that measures ER visits directly is the strongest kind of evidence.
One patient's story, a seller's slogan, and a doctor's preference are weaker and may be biased.

q:
Councilmember Reyes argues that the city needs more cooling-center space. Last July, the city's two cooling centers turned away 140 people because they were full. Heat-related visits to the county hospital's emergency room doubled during the July heat wave. Reyes also notes that she grew up without air conditioning. The current centers offer free Wi-Fi.

Which statements from the passage provide evidence that the city needs more cooling-center space? Select all that apply.
o: The two centers turned away 140 people because they were full.
Heat-related ER visits doubled during the heat wave.
Reyes grew up without air conditioning.
The current centers offer free Wi-Fi.
Reyes is a member of the city council.
e: People being turned away shows the centers are too small, and doubled ER visits show many residents needed relief from the heat.
Reyes's childhood, the Wi-Fi, and her job title do not show a need for more space.

q: "This textbook is reliable because it says it is the most trustworthy textbook available." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
o: It uses the claim itself as its own proof.
It draws a conclusion from one example.
It attacks the author of a different textbook.
e: This is circular reasoning: the book's reliability is "proven" only by the book's own statement about itself.

q:
Students should eat breakfast before morning exams. In one study, students who ate breakfast scored higher on morning tests than students who skipped it.

Which statement is the evidence in this argument?
o: Students should eat breakfast before morning exams.
Morning exams cause many students a great deal of stress and worry.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day for growing students.
In one study, breakfast eaters scored higher on morning tests.
e: The study result is the support offered for the claim.
"Students should eat breakfast" is the claim itself, and the other choices do not appear in the passage.

q: "We shouldn't listen to Ms. Tran's plan for the clinic. She drives an old car and can't even keep her lawn mowed." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
o: It relies on statistics that are out of date.
It attacks the person instead of responding to her plan.
It offers only two possible choices when there are more.
It uses the claim itself as the proof for the claim.
e: This is an ad hominem attack: her car and lawn have nothing to do with whether her clinic plan is good.

q:
All patients on the cardiac unit wear a heart monitor. Mr. Kim is wearing a heart monitor.

Based only on these statements, what can be concluded?
o: Mr. Kim is on the cardiac unit.
Mr. Kim is not on the cardiac unit.
Every patient with a heart monitor is on the cardiac unit.
It cannot be determined whether Mr. Kim is on the cardiac unit.
e: The statements say cardiac patients wear monitors, NOT that only cardiac patients wear them.
Patients on other units, such as the ER, may also wear monitors, so Mr. Kim's unit cannot be determined.
t: "All A are B" does not mean "all B are A."

q:
Our town of 3,000 people needs a pharmacy. The nearest one is 20 miles away, and the county bus runs only twice a day. Older residents sometimes go days without their medicine because they cannot get a ride.

Which sentence, if added, would most strengthen the argument?
o: 60 percent of older residents in a survey had missed doses because they could not reach a pharmacy.
Pharmacists earn some of the highest salaries in health care, so the job would easily attract workers.
The town already has two grocery stores, a gas station, and a small public library downtown.
Some residents enjoy driving 20 miles to the city to shop and see a movie on weekends.
e: The survey adds hard numbers that show how often the distance causes missed medicine.
Salaries and grocery stores are irrelevant, and residents who enjoy driving weakens rather than strengthens the case.

q: Put the parts of this argument in the most logical order, from the claim to the conclusion.
o: Our college should add an evening section of anatomy.
Last semester, 85 students were on the waiting list for the only evening section.
Some may say that no instructors are available to teach at night.
However, two part-time instructors have already offered to teach the class.
Adding the section would help working students stay on track for nursing school.
e: A strong argument usually moves from claim, to evidence, to a counterargument, to a rebuttal ("However..."), to a conclusion.
The counterargument must come before the "However" sentence that answers it.

q:
Passage 1
Drinking coffee in moderation, about three to four cups a day, has been linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes in several large studies. Coffee also contains antioxidants, substances that help protect cells from damage. Passage 2
While moderate coffee drinking appears to be safe for most adults, some people should be careful. Pregnant women are advised to limit caffeine to about 200 mg a day, roughly two small cups of coffee. People who have anxiety or trouble sleeping may also feel better if they cut back. With which statement would both authors most likely agree?
o: Pregnant women should avoid coffee completely.
Coffee causes anxiety in most people who drink it.
Moderate coffee drinking can be part of a healthy adult's routine.
Coffee prevents type 2 diabetes in everyone who drinks it.
e: Passage 1 links moderate coffee to health benefits, and Passage 2 says moderate drinking "appears to be safe for most adults."
Passage 2 says pregnant women should LIMIT caffeine, not avoid it. Neither author says coffee causes anxiety in most people or prevents diabetes in everyone.

q:
Passage 1
Drinking coffee in moderation, about three to four cups a day, has been linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes in several large studies. Coffee also contains antioxidants, substances that help protect cells from damage. Passage 2
While moderate coffee drinking appears to be safe for most adults, some people should be careful. Pregnant women are advised to limit caffeine to about 200 mg a day, roughly two small cups of coffee. People who have anxiety or trouble sleeping may also feel better if they cut back. How does Passage 2 differ from Passage 1?
o: Passage 2 argues that coffee is harmful for all adults, while Passage 1 says it is completely safe.
Passage 2 focuses on who may need to limit caffeine; Passage 1 focuses on possible benefits.
Passage 2 gives the results of large research studies, while Passage 1 gives only personal opinions.
Passage 2 tells a personal story, while Passage 1 gives directions.
e: Passage 1 discusses benefits (lower diabetes risk, antioxidants). Passage 2 discusses cautions for certain groups.
Passage 2 does not call coffee harmful for all adults; it says it is safe for most. Passage 1, not Passage 2, cites studies.

q:
Passage 1
(From a family diary) March 3. The dust came again today. Mama hung wet sheets over the windows, but by supper our plates were gritty and Baby June would not stop coughing. Papa says if it doesn't rain by summer, we'll load the truck and head for California. Passage 2
During the 1930s, severe drought and poor farming practices in the southern Great Plains led to massive dust storms, a period known as the Dust Bowl. Hundreds of thousands of people moved west, many of them to California's Central Valley, in search of farm work. Which statement best describes the two passages?
o: Passage 1 is a secondary source, and Passage 2 is a primary source.
Passage 1 is a primary source, and Passage 2 is a secondary source.
e: A diary written by someone living through an event is a primary source.
A textbook-style summary written later about the period is a secondary source.
t: Primary = written by someone who was there. Secondary = written later, about it.

q:
Passage 1
(From a family diary) March 3. The dust came again today. Mama hung wet sheets over the windows, but by supper our plates were gritty and Baby June would not stop coughing. Papa says if it doesn't rain by summer, we'll load the truck and head for California. Passage 2
During the 1930s, severe drought and poor farming practices in the southern Great Plains led to massive dust storms, a period known as the Dust Bowl. Hundreds of thousands of people moved west, many of them to California's Central Valley, in search of farm work. What information does Passage 2 provide that Passage 1 does not?
o: The causes of the dust storms
How families tried to keep dust out of their homes
How the dust affected a young child
A family's plan to move to California
e: Passage 2 names drought and poor farming practices as causes; Passage 1 never explains why the storms happened.
The wet sheets, the coughing baby, and the plan to move are all details from Passage 1.

q:
Passage 1
Our district should require every high school student to complete 40 hours of community service before graduating. Service teaches responsibility and connects teens with their neighbors in ways a classroom cannot. Passage 2
Requiring community service sounds noble, but many of our students already work after school to help support their families. Volunteer hours should be encouraged and celebrated, not required for a diploma. Which statement best describes how the authors' views are related?
o: The author of Passage 2 believes that community service is harmful to most teens.
Both authors think that community service should be required for every graduate.
The author of Passage 1 opposes community service.
Both value service, but they disagree about whether it should be required.
e: Passage 1 wants service required; Passage 2 says it should be "encouraged and celebrated, not required."
Passage 2 still values service, so it does not call it harmful.

q:
Passage 1
Our district should require every high school student to complete 40 hours of community service before graduating. Service teaches responsibility and connects teens with their neighbors in ways a classroom cannot. Passage 2
Requiring community service sounds noble, but many of our students already work after school to help support their families. Volunteer hours should be encouraged and celebrated, not required for a diploma. How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to the claim in Passage 1 that service "teaches responsibility"?
o: Responsibility is not an especially important quality for high school students.
Students who work to help their families already learn responsibility.
Students should be required to complete 80 hours of service instead.
Most teens today do not have any real connection to their neighbors.
e: Passage 2 points out that many students already work to help their families, which is itself a responsible role.
Passage 2 never dismisses responsibility or asks for more hours, and it says nothing about neighbors.

q:
Passage 1
Never miss a dose again! The DoseKeeper smart pill organizer beeps loudly at every dose time and lights up the right compartment. Thousands of happy customers trust DoseKeeper. Order today and get free shipping! Passage 2
I tested the DoseKeeper for a month with my father, who has arthritis. The alarm was loud and never failed. However, the small plastic lids were so hard to open that he needed my help with almost every dose. A woman is deciding whether to buy the DoseKeeper for her mother, who has arthritis in her hands. Why is Passage 2 more useful for her decision?
o: It was written by the company that makes and sells the DoseKeeper.
It offers free shipping if she orders the product today.
It mentions that thousands of happy customers trust the product.
It reports a real user's test, including a problem for arthritis.
e: Passage 2 is a user's review that reports a problem (hard-to-open lids) that matters for someone with arthritis.
Passage 1 is an advertisement written to sell the product, and it is the one with free shipping and "thousands of happy customers."

q:
Passage 1
Never miss a dose again! The DoseKeeper smart pill organizer beeps loudly at every dose time and lights up the right compartment. Thousands of happy customers trust DoseKeeper. Order today and get free shipping! Passage 2
I tested the DoseKeeper for a month with my father, who has arthritis. The alarm was loud and never failed. However, the small plastic lids were so hard to open that he needed my help with almost every dose. Which statement about the two passages is accurate?
o: Both passages mention only the positive features of the DoseKeeper organizer.
Passage 1 mentions only positives; Passage 2 mentions a positive and a negative.
Passage 1 mentions a drawback of the product, while Passage 2 does not mention any.
Both passages are written to sell the product.
e: Passage 1 is an ad with only praise. Passage 2 praises the alarm but criticizes the lids.

q:
Passage 1
(Flyer printed in September) Free flu shots! Walk-in clinic every Saturday, 9 a.m. to noon, at the County Health Department. Passage 2
(Health Department website, updated October 20) Because of high demand, Saturday flu clinic hours are extended to 9 a.m.–3 p.m. through November. A reader sees both sources on October 25. What is the best conclusion about Saturday hours in November?
o: The clinic will be open from 9 a.m. to noon, because the flyer was printed first.
The clinic will be closed on Saturdays in November.
The clinic will be open from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., because Passage 2 is more recent.
The hours cannot be known, because the two sources disagree.
e: When sources conflict, check the dates. The website was updated in October, after the September flyer.
The newer source explains the change ("hours are extended"), so 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. is the best conclusion.
t: When two sources disagree, look for dates and the more authoritative source.

q:
Passage 1
Valley fever spores are most common in dry, undisturbed soil. They become airborne when the soil is disturbed by wind, digging, or farm work. Passage 2
A construction company in Kern County reported several cases of valley fever among its workers after they graded a large site during a windy, dry month. Which conclusion is best supported by the two passages together?
o: Activities that disturb dry soil can increase people's exposure to valley fever.
Valley fever affects only construction workers.
Wind alone is the cause of every valley fever case.
Kern County has more valley fever cases each year than any other county in California.
e: Passage 1 explains that disturbing soil releases spores, and Passage 2 gives an example: workers got sick after grading dry, windy ground.
Neither passage says only construction workers get sick or that wind ALONE causes every case, and no counties are compared.

q:
Passage 1
The new hospital parking fees are an outrage. Sick people and their families are being nickel-and-dimed at the worst moments of their lives. Passage 2
The hospital has introduced parking fees of $2 per hour, with a daily maximum of $10. Patients receiving chemotherapy or dialysis may park free with a validated ticket. Which best describes the difference in tone between the passages?
o: Passage 1 is angry and emotional; Passage 2 is calm and factual.
Passage 1 is calm and neutral; Passage 2 is angry and emotional.
Both passages are lighthearted and humorous in tone.
Both passages are neutral and factual, with no emotion.
e: Words like "outrage" and "nickel-and-dimed" show anger in Passage 1. Passage 2 simply states the fees and exceptions.

q:
Passage 1
The new hospital parking fees are an outrage. Sick people and their families are being nickel-and-dimed at the worst moments of their lives. Passage 2
The hospital has introduced parking fees of $2 per hour, with a daily maximum of $10. Patients receiving chemotherapy or dialysis may park free with a validated ticket. Which detail from Passage 2 most directly responds to the concern raised in Passage 1?
o: The hospital has recently introduced new parking fees.
Parking tickets are issued at the gate when drivers arrive.
Chemotherapy and dialysis patients may park free.
e: Passage 1 worries about charging sick people; the free parking for patients in ongoing treatment speaks directly to that concern.
The hourly fee and the fact that fees exist are what Passage 1 is complaining about, and nothing in Passage 2 mentions a parking gate.

q:
Passage 1
Adults who regularly sleep fewer than seven hours a night have higher rates of obesity, heart disease, and depression. Researchers believe sleep gives the body time to repair tissue and to balance the hormones that control appetite. Passage 2
Night-shift nurses often sleep fewer hours than day-shift nurses and report more weight gain. Experts suggest dark, cool bedrooms and a consistent sleep schedule, even on days off. Which statements are supported by BOTH passages? Select all that apply.
o: Too little sleep may be linked to weight gain.
A consistent sleep schedule is recommended.
Getting too little sleep may affect health.
e: Passage 1 links short sleep to obesity, and Passage 2 links fewer hours of sleep to weight gain, so both support a link to weight and to health.
Only Passage 2 recommends a consistent schedule, only Passage 1 mentions appetite hormones, and neither says night shifts cause depression.
t: For "both passages" questions, test each choice against Passage 1 AND Passage 2.

q: A student is writing a report on how the 1918 flu affected daily life in Fresno. Which source would be most useful?
o: A general encyclopedia article about how flu viruses copy themselves
A 1918 Fresno newspaper article announcing that schools would close
A recent magazine article about how modern flu vaccines are developed
A popular novel about a family living through the 1918 flu in New York City
e: A local newspaper from 1918 is a primary source about daily life in Fresno at that time.
The other sources cover a different topic, a different time, or a different place, and a novel is fiction.

q:
Passage 1
Hydrologists estimate that farms and towns in the valley pump far more groundwater each year than rain and rivers replace. Without limits, wells will keep running dry and the land will keep sinking. Passage 2
My family has farmed here for four generations. If the state cuts our pumping, we'll have to leave half our land unplanted and lay off workers who have been with us for decades. Which best describes the relationship between the two passages?
o: Passage 2 uses new data from local farms to prove that the estimates in Passage 1 are wrong.
Both passages argue that the state should not place any limits on groundwater pumping.
Passage 1 explains why limits may be needed; Passage 2 shows the hardship limits could cause.
Passage 1 tells a personal family story, while Passage 2 gives scientific estimates from experts.
e: Passage 1 gives the scientific case for limits; Passage 2 gives a farmer's view of their cost.
Passage 2 does not dispute the data, and Passage 1 supports limits. The last choice reverses the two passages.

q:
Passage 1
Hydrologists estimate that farms and towns in the valley pump far more groundwater each year than rain and rivers replace. Without limits, wells will keep running dry and the land will keep sinking. Passage 2
My family has farmed here for four generations. If the state cuts our pumping, we'll have to leave half our land unplanted and lay off workers who have been with us for decades. What kind of evidence does each author mainly use?
o: Passage 1 uses personal experience; Passage 2 uses expert estimates.
Both passages rely mainly on statistics.
Both passages rely mainly on personal stories.
Passage 1 uses expert estimates; Passage 2 uses personal experience.
e: Passage 1 cites what hydrologists (experts) estimate. Passage 2 speaks from the writer's own family and farm.

q:
Passage 1
(From a first-aid manual) Cool a minor burn under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes. Do not put ice, butter, or oil on a fresh burn. Passage 2
(From a personal blog) My grandma always put butter on our burns, and it worked great for us! Which statement best evaluates the two sources?
o: Passage 2 is more reliable because the grandmother used her method successfully for many years.
Both sources are equally reliable because both of them describe how to treat minor burns.
Passage 1 is more reliable because it comes from a first-aid manual, not one family's experience.
Neither source can be trusted, because the two sources give advice that disagrees.
e: A first-aid manual reflects expert guidance. A single family's experience is an anecdote, not evidence.
Disagreement does not make both sources useless; it means the reader should weigh which is more credible.

q:
Passage 1
The clinic will hold a free diabetes screening on Saturday, May 10, from 9 a.m. to noon in the community room. Passage 2
(Email from the screening coordinator) Reminder: Our diabetes screening is this Saturday. Please arrive 10 minutes early to fill out forms, and do not eat for 8 hours before your screening. What information appears in Passage 2 but NOT in Passage 1?
o: The screening is free for everyone who attends.
Patients should not eat for 8 hours beforehand.
The screening takes place in the clinic's community room.
The screening is held on a Saturday.
e: Only the coordinator's email gives the fasting instruction and the advice to arrive early.
"Free" and "community room" appear only in Passage 1, and both passages say Saturday.

q:
Passage 1
Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood all around your body, day and night, even while you sleep. Passage 2
The heart has four chambers. The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body and passes it to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps it out to the body. Which statement best describes a difference between the passages?
o: Passage 2 gives more detailed, technical information about blood flow.
Passage 1 is more technical than Passage 2.
Passage 2 is written mainly to persuade the reader to exercise.
Passage 1 contradicts some of the information given in Passage 2.
e: Passage 2 names chambers and traces the path of blood. Passage 1 is a simple overview, perhaps for children.
Neither passage is persuasive, and the two do not contradict each other.

q:
Passage 1
The college opened its new nursing simulation lab in 2019, two years after voters approved a bond measure to pay for it. Passage 2
Planning for the simulation lab began in 2015, when instructors noticed that students were getting fewer practice hours in local hospitals. The first class of students trained in the new lab graduated in 2021. Using information from both passages, put the events in order from first to last.
o: The first class trained in the lab graduated.
e: Passage 2: planning began in 2015. Passage 1: the lab opened in 2019, two years after the bond, so the bond passed in 2017.
Passage 2: the first class graduated in 2021. Order: 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021.

q:
A heat-safety article warns that outdoor workers face the greatest risk during the hottest month of the year.
Average daily high temperature, Fresno (approximate)
MonthMayJuneJulyAugustSeptember
Average high (°F)88961019993
According to the table, which month carries the greatest risk?
e: The highest average high in the table is 101 °F, in July.

q:
The clinic director claims that the flu vaccination rate increased every year from 2021 to 2025.
Flu vaccination rate, adults at one clinic
Year20212022202320242025
Adults vaccinated (%)4245444953
Does the table support the director's claim?
o: Yes, because the rate was higher in 2025 than in 2021.
Yes, because the rate went up by the same amount each year.
No, because the rate went down from 2024 to 2025.
No, because the rate dropped from 2022 to 2023.
e: "Every year" means no decreases at all. The rate fell from 45% in 2022 to 44% in 2023.
A higher rate overall does not make "every year" true. 2024 to 2025 was an increase (49% to 53%).
t: Test absolute words like "every" and "always" against EVERY data point.

q: A community clinic plans to add a new program for the age group it serves most. Based on the chart, which age group will the program serve?
e: The tallest bar is ages 50–64, with 220 patients.
Ages 18–34 (200) is close but smaller.

q:
A patient with high blood pressure has been told to keep her sodium under 1,500 mg per day. For lunch, she eats one serving of soup and one serving of crackers.
Food (1 serving)Sodium (mg)
Chicken noodle soup, 1 cup890
Crackers, 5 crackers180
Cheddar cheese, 1 oz175
Apple, 1 medium2
Based on the passage and the table, about how much sodium can she still have for the rest of the day?
e: Lunch sodium: 890 mg + 180 mg = 1,070 mg.
Remaining: 1,500 mg − 1,070 mg = 430 mg.
1,070 mg is the lunch total, not what is left; 610 mg forgets the crackers; 255 mg also subtracts the cheese, which she did not eat.

q:
A student claims that students who sleep more get higher exam scores. She collected the data below from four classmates.
StudentAverage sleep (hours)Exam score
A568
B674
C781
D885
Which statement best describes how the data relate to the claim?
o: The data show that the claim is false.
The data prove that getting more sleep causes higher exam scores.
The data have nothing to do with the claim about sleep.
The data match the claim, but four students are too few to prove it.
e: Scores rise as sleep increases, so the pattern fits the claim.
But four students is a very small sample, and a pattern alone does not prove cause and effect.

q:
A city wants to cut its total water use by 20 percent this summer. The mayor proposes cutting landscaping water use in half and making no other changes.
UseShare of city water use
Landscaping (lawns, gardens)50%
Indoor household use35%
Businesses10%
Leaks5%
Based on the table, would the mayor's plan meet the goal?
o: No, because total use would drop by only 10 percent.
Yes, because total use would drop by 25 percent.
No, because landscaping is only half of all water use.
Yes, because total use would drop by 50 percent.
e: Landscaping is 50% of all use. Cutting it in half saves 50% × ½ = 25% of the total.
25% is more than the 20% goal, so the plan works. 50% is the trap of confusing the share with the savings.

q: The nurse's note says: "Acetaminophen given at 10 a.m. for fever." Based on the note and the graph, what happened to the patient's temperature after the medicine was given?
e: The highest point is at 10 a.m. (about 102.4 °F). After that, every reading is lower, down to about 99 °F at 4 p.m.

q:
Lupe wants to burn at least 200 calories in a 30-minute workout, but she does not have access to a pool.
Activity (30 minutes)Approximate calories burned*
Walking, brisk150
Gardening165
Swimming215
Bicycling, moderate260
*for a 155-lb adult Based on the passage and the table, which activity should Lupe choose?
e: Only swimming (215) and bicycling (260) reach 200 calories.
Lupe has no pool, so bicycling is the activity that meets both conditions.

q:
A clinic manager wrote: "Our waits are longest at the beginning and end of the week, so we should add a provider on those days."
DayMonTueWedThuFri
Average wait (minutes)4831252952
Do the data support the manager's statement about wait times?
o: No, because Wednesday has the longest wait.
Yes, because Monday and Friday have the longest waits.
Yes, because Tuesday has the longest wait.
No, because the waits are about the same every day.
e: Monday (48 min) and Friday (52 min) are much longer than Tuesday through Thursday (25–31 min).
Wednesday actually has the SHORTEST wait.

q:
The student newspaper surveyed 200 students about how they get to campus.
Survey of 200 students
How students get to campusPercent
Drive alone55%
Bus20%
Bike or walk15%
Carpool10%
How many of the students surveyed ride the bus?
e: 20 is the percent, not the number of students; 110 is the number who drive alone.

q:
A brochure for Valley Gym claims that "our members lose an average of 10 pounds in their first three months."
Valley Gym member survey
Members surveyed30
Average weight change after 3 months−4 lb
Members who lost 10 lb or more12
Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
o: The survey proves that the brochure's claim about weight loss is accurate.
Most of the members surveyed lost 10 pounds or more in three months.
The survey does not support the brochure's claim about average loss.
e: The survey's average change is −4 lb (a loss of 4 pounds), not 10 pounds.
Only 12 of 30 members (40%) lost 10 pounds or more, which is less than half.
An average loss of 4 lb does not suggest that most members gained weight.

q:
The nurse is preparing the patient's 0800 medications.
Medication administration record
MedicationScheduled times
Metformin 500 mg0800, 1800
Lisinopril 10 mg0800
Atorvastatin 20 mg2100
Which medications should the nurse prepare?
e: 0800 appears next to both metformin and lisinopril.
Atorvastatin is scheduled for 2100 (9 p.m.).

q: A news report says valley fever cases in Example County "jumped the most from 2022 to 2023." Based on the chart, is the report correct?
o: No; the largest increase was from 2019 to 2020, when cases rose by 120.
Yes; the rise of 220 cases was the largest one-year increase.
No; the largest increase was from 2020 to 2021.
e: The +220 rise from 480 to 700 is the largest, so the report is correct.

q:
Ana's father needs a hospital that has a cardiac unit and is no more than 30 miles from home.
HospitalCardiac unit?Distance from home
Hospital AYes12 miles
Hospital BNo5 miles
Hospital CYes28 miles
Hospital DYes41 miles
Hospital ENo18 miles
Which hospitals meet both requirements? Select all that apply.
e: Hospitals A (12 miles) and C (28 miles) have cardiac units and are within 30 miles.
B and E have no cardiac unit, and D is 41 miles away.

q:
An article about sleep includes the table below.
Survey of college students
Daily screen time after 9 p.m.Average sleep (hours)
Less than 30 minutes7.8
30–60 minutes7.1
1–2 hours6.5
More than 2 hours5.9
Which statement best describes the relationship shown in the table?
o: As late-night screen time increases, average sleep decreases.
As late-night screen time increases, average sleep increases.
Late-night screen time has no relationship to sleep.
Students with the most screen time sleep about 7.8 hours.
e: Moving down the table, screen time goes up while sleep goes down (7.8 to 5.9 hours): a negative relationship.
7.8 hours goes with the LEAST screen time.

q:
Health guidelines suggest limiting added sugars to less than 10 percent of daily calories. For a 2,000-calorie diet, that is about 50 grams of added sugar per day. Maya drinks one cola and one sports drink in a day.
Drink (12 fl oz)Added sugars (g)
Cola39
Sweet tea32
Sports drink21
Sparkling water0
Based on the passage and the table, which statement is true?
o: Maya's drinks contain 60 g of added sugar, which is under the limit.
Maya's drinks contain 39 g of added sugar, which is under the limit.
Maya's drinks contain 60 g of added sugar, which is over the limit.
Maya's drinks contain exactly 50 g of added sugar.
e: Cola 39 g + sports drink 21 g = 60 g.
60 g is more than the suggested 50 g limit, even before she eats any food.

q:
Ty works every day and can study only after his shift ends at 5:30 p.m.
DayLibrary hours
Monday–Thursday8 a.m.–8 p.m.
Friday8 a.m.–5 p.m.
Saturday10 a.m.–2 p.m.
SundayClosed
On which days can Ty study at the library after his shift?
e: The library is open after 5:30 p.m. only Monday–Thursday (until 8 p.m.).
It closes at 5 p.m. on Friday, at 2 p.m. on Saturday, and is closed Sunday.

q:
Most newborns lose a little weight in their first few days, but they usually return to their birth weight by about 2 weeks of age.
Infant weight checks
AgeWeight (lb)
Birth7.5
2 weeks7.8
1 month9.0
2 months11.2
Is this infant's growth consistent with the passage?
o: No; the infant did not lose any weight after birth.
Yes; by 2 weeks the infant weighed more than at birth.
No; the infant weighed less at 2 weeks than at birth.
Yes; the infant doubled its birth weight by 1 month.
e: At 2 weeks the infant weighed 7.8 lb, above the birth weight of 7.5 lb, which matches "return to birth weight by about 2 weeks."
The table does not show the first few days, so we cannot say the infant never lost weight. 9.0 lb is not double 7.5 lb.

q:
One morning, Jess drinks 4 fl oz of brewed coffee, 16 fl oz of black tea, 8 fl oz of an energy drink, and 16 fl oz of green tea.
Approximate caffeine content
Drink (per 8 fl oz)Caffeine (mg)
Brewed coffee95
Energy drink80
Black tea47
Green tea28
Put the drinks in order from the MOST caffeine Jess got to the LEAST.
e: Adjust each drink for the amount: coffee 4 oz = ½ × 95 = 47.5 mg; black tea 16 oz = 2 × 47 = 94 mg; energy drink 8 oz = 80 mg; green tea 16 oz = 2 × 28 = 56 mg.
Most to least: black tea (94), energy drink (80), green tea (56), coffee (47.5). Coffee has the most per 8 oz, but Jess drank only half a serving.

q:
A state grant will go to the county with the lowest rate of health insurance.
CountyResidents with health insurance
County A88%
County B92%
County C85%
County D90%
Which county will receive the grant?
e: County C has the lowest insured rate, 85%.
County B has the HIGHEST rate, the opposite of what the grant requires.

q: In anatomical position, the wrist is ______ to the elbow.
e: Proximal and distal compare positions along a limb: proximal = closer to where the limb attaches to the trunk, distal = farther away.
The wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow is, so the wrist is distal to the elbow.
"Superior" is wrong: in anatomical position the arms hang down, so the wrist is below the elbow.
t: Distal sounds like "distance": farther from the trunk.

q: Which plane divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions?
e: A frontal (coronal) plane runs side to side, like a crown headband, separating front from back.
Sagittal and midsagittal planes divide left from right; a transverse plane divides superior from inferior.

q: A CT scan shows a "slice" of the abdomen that separates the body into upper and lower portions. Which plane is this?
e: A transverse plane runs horizontally and divides the body into superior and inferior parts.
Most CT and MRI images of the trunk are viewed as transverse (cross-sectional) slices.
t: Transverse = "traverse across" the body, like slicing a loaf of bread.

q: The heart and lungs are located in which body cavity?
e: The thoracic (chest) cavity is the part of the ventral cavity above the diaphragm.
It contains the lungs (in pleural cavities) and the heart (in the pericardial cavity within the mediastinum).

q: A patient at a Visalia urgent care has fever and pain that began near the navel and has moved to the lower right abdomen. Appendicitis is suspected. In which abdominopelvic quadrant is the appendix located?
e: The appendix hangs from the cecum, the first part of the large intestine, in the right lower quadrant (RLQ).
Right and left always refer to the patient's right and left, not the viewer's.
t: Always use the PATIENT's right and left, as if you are facing them.

q: What is the smallest level of organization that can carry out all the functions of life?
e: Molecules (like DNA or proteins) are not alive by themselves.
The cell is the smallest living unit; tissues and organs are built from many cells.

q: Put these levels of structural organization in order from simplest (smallest) to most complex.
e: Atoms and molecules form cells.
Similar cells working together form a tissue.
Two or more tissue types form an organ, and organs working together form an organ system.
t: Remember: Chemicals Can Team Up Over Systems (Chemical, Cell, Tissue, Organ, System).

q: Which tissue type covers body surfaces, lines body cavities and hollow organs, and forms glands?
e: Epithelial tissue forms sheets that cover and line surfaces (skin epidermis, lining of the GI tract) and forms glands.
Connective tissue supports and binds; muscle contracts; nervous tissue conducts signals.
t: Epithelium = "upon" a surface: it covers, lines, and forms glands.

q: Which of the following are types of connective tissue? Select all that apply.
e: Connective tissues have cells scattered in an extracellular matrix: blood (liquid plasma matrix), bone (mineralized matrix), and adipose tissue are all connective tissue.
The epidermis is epithelial tissue, and cardiac muscle is muscle tissue.
t: If it has cells floating in a "matrix" (even a liquid one), think connective tissue.

q: The walls of the alveoli (air sacs) in the lungs are made of simple squamous epithelium. Which feature of this tissue best explains why it is found there?
o: Many stacked layers of cells protect the lungs from abrasion
Cilia on the cells sweep mucus and trapped dust out of the lungs
A single layer of thin, flat cells allows rapid diffusion of gases
Tall columnar cells secrete large amounts of mucus into the sacs
e: "Simple" means one cell layer and "squamous" means flat cells, so the barrier is extremely thin.
A thin barrier lets O₂ and CO₂ diffuse quickly between air and blood.
Stacked (stratified) layers protect areas like the skin; ciliated and mucus-secreting cells line the larger airways, not the alveoli.
t: Structure fits function: thin tissue where things must cross, thick tissue where things must be protected.

q: Which of the following is an example of negative feedback?
o: Oxytocin release that strengthens uterine contractions during labor
