Sweating when body temperature rises above normal
Activated platelets attracting more platelets to a forming clot
Milk release that increases as an infant continues to nurse
e: Negative feedback reverses a change and brings a variable back toward its set point.
Sweating cools the body, reversing the rise in temperature.
The other three are positive feedback: the response amplifies the original change until an event (birth, clot, feeding) ends it.

q: During labor, stretching of the cervix triggers release of a hormone that makes uterine contractions stronger, which stretches the cervix even more. Which hormone and which type of feedback does this describe?
e: The hormone that stimulates uterine contractions is oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary.
The response (stronger contractions) increases the original stimulus (cervical stretch), so it is positive feedback; it stops when the baby is delivered.
Prolactin stimulates milk production, and progesterone actually helps keep the uterus quiet during pregnancy.

q: In a homeostatic feedback loop, which component detects a change in the internal environment?
e: The receptor senses the change and sends information to the control center.
The control center compares the value to the set point, and the effector (a muscle or gland) carries out the response.
t: Order of a loop: Receptor → Control center → Effector (R-C-E).

q: A phlebotomist draws blood from a vein in the antecubital region. Where is this?
e: Antecubital means "in front of the elbow" (ante = before, cubitus = elbow).
The back of the knee is the popliteal region, the armpit is the axillary region, and the groin is the inguinal region.
t: Ante- means before or in front; cubitus is the elbow.

q: A nurse checks for a pulse in the hollow behind the knee. Which pulse is this?
e: The popliteal region is the posterior knee, where the popliteal artery can be felt.
The femoral pulse is in the groin, the brachial pulse is in the arm near the elbow, and the radial pulse is at the thumb side of the wrist.

q: Which of the following organs are located in the abdominopelvic cavity? Select all that apply.
e: The abdominopelvic cavity lies below the diaphragm.
The liver and small intestine are in the abdominal portion; the urinary bladder is in the pelvic portion.
The lungs are in the thoracic cavity, and the thyroid gland is in the neck, outside the ventral body cavity.

q: The ventral body cavity is divided into the thoracic cavity and the abdominopelvic cavity by a dome-shaped muscle called the ______.
e: The diaphragm separates the chest (thoracic) cavity above from the abdominopelvic cavity below.
It is also the main muscle of breathing.

mx.pleura: The pleura lines the lungs. The muscle that separates the cavities is the diaphragm.
mx.mediastinum: The mediastinum is the central part of the thoracic cavity, not a dividing muscle.

q: Which serous membrane is attached directly to the outer surface of each lung?
e: Visceral layers cover organs (viscera); parietal layers line the cavity walls.
"Pleura" refers to the lungs, "pericardium" to the heart, and "peritoneum" to the abdominal cavity.
So the membrane on the lung surface is the visceral pleura.
t: Visceral = on the viscera (organ); Parietal = on the wall (think "partition").

q: Which statement uses a directional term INCORRECTLY for a person in anatomical position?
o: The sternum is medial to the arms.
The skin is superficial to the skeletal muscles.
The nose is anterior to the ears.
The knee is proximal to the hip.
e: The hip is closer to the trunk than the knee, so the knee is distal to the hip, not proximal.
The sternum is near the midline (medial), the skin is closer to the surface (superficial), and the nose is in front of (anterior to) the ears, so those statements are correct.

q: Homeostasis is best described as
o: keeping every body variable at one exact value at every moment of the day
the body's repair response that occurs only after an injury or infection
keeping internal conditions within a stable range despite outside changes
the steady growth of new cells to replace old, worn-out ones
e: Homeostasis means keeping internal conditions (temperature, blood glucose, pH) within a narrow normal range.
Values fluctuate around a set point; they are not frozen at one exact number.

q: The spinal cord is protected within which body cavity?
e: The dorsal body cavity has two parts: the cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral cavity (spinal cord).
The thoracic, pelvic, and pericardial cavities are all parts of the ventral body cavity.

q: A patient's chart says a wound is located on the "plantar" surface. Where should the nurse look?
e: Plantar refers to the sole of the foot (think "planting" your foot on the ground).
The palm is the palmar surface, the back of the hand is dorsal, and the top of the head is the cranial or parietal region.

q: Put these structures in the order that oxygen-poor blood passes through them on its way from the body to the lungs.
e: Oxygen-poor blood from the body returns through the venae cavae into the right atrium.
It passes the tricuspid (right AV) valve into the right ventricle.
The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries toward the lungs.
t: Remember: you "try" (tricuspid) before you "bi" (bicuspid/mitral): right side first, then left.

q: Put these structures in the order that oxygen-rich blood passes through them, starting from the lungs.
e: Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
It flows through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle.
The left ventricle pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body.

q: Which vessel carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs?
e: Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart, even when that blood is low in oxygen.
The pulmonary arteries take oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; the pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood back.
t: Arteries = Away from the heart. Oxygen level does not decide the name.

q: Which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall?
e: The left ventricle pumps blood through the entire systemic circulation, which has much higher resistance than the lungs.
It needs the most muscle (myocardium) to generate that pressure.
The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, and the atria just push blood into the ventricles.

q: Which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker?
e: The SA node in the wall of the right atrium fires on its own fastest, so it sets the heart rate.
The AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers conduct the signal it starts.

q: Put the parts of the cardiac conduction system in the order the electrical impulse travels through them.
e: The impulse starts at the SA node and spreads across the atria, which contract.
The AV node briefly delays it so the ventricles can fill.
It then travels down the bundle of His, the bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers, which make the ventricles contract from the apex upward.

q: Which valve is located between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
e: The left atrioventricular valve has two cusps, so it is called the bicuspid or mitral valve.
The tricuspid valve is on the right side; the aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles.

q: Exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and wastes between the blood and body tissues takes place across the walls of which vessels?
e: Capillary walls are a single layer of endothelial cells, thin enough for substances to diffuse through.
Arteries, arterioles, and veins have thicker walls and mainly serve to carry blood.
t: Capillary walls are one cell thick: thin walls, fast exchange.

q: Which of the following are formed elements (cells or cell fragments) of the blood? Select all that apply.
e: Formed elements are the cells and cell fragments: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets (fragments of megakaryocytes).
Albumin (a plasma protein) and water are parts of plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

q: A patient with a very low platelet count is at greatest risk for which problem?
e: Platelets (thrombocytes) form a plug at an injury and help start clotting.
Too few platelets means bleeding is hard to stop.
Frequent infections suggest low white blood cells; low oxygen suggests too few red blood cells (anemia).

q: A patient has left-sided heart failure, meaning the left ventricle cannot pump blood forward effectively. Fluid will most likely back up into which organs first?
e: Blood returning from the lungs enters the left side of the heart.
If the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the pulmonary veins and lungs, causing pulmonary congestion and shortness of breath.
Swelling of the ankles, feet, and liver is typical of right-sided failure, because blood backs up into the systemic veins.
t: Left fails → Lungs (both start with L). Right fails → the rest of the body.

q: A patient's blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. What does the 128 represent?
o: Pressure in the arteries when the ventricles relax (diastolic)
The number of times the heart beats per minute
The pressure inside the right atrium of the heart
Pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract (systolic)
e: The top number is systolic pressure: the peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction (systole).
The bottom number (82) is diastolic pressure, during ventricular relaxation.
Heart rate is measured separately in beats per minute.
t: Systolic = Squeeze (top number); Diastolic = Dilate/relax (bottom number).

q: Why do many veins in the legs contain valves?
o: To raise blood pressure in the veins above arterial pressure
To allow gas exchange with surrounding tissues
To prevent blood from flowing backward away from the heart
To pump blood the way the heart does
e: Blood pressure in veins is low, and blood in the legs must return to the heart against gravity.
One-way valves keep blood moving toward the heart while skeletal muscles squeeze the veins.
Valves do not pump on their own; the surrounding muscle contractions provide the push.

q: A blockage in a coronary artery most directly deprives which tissue of oxygen?
o: The inner lining of the aorta
e: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself.
A blocked coronary artery causes a myocardial infarction (heart attack), in which heart muscle cells die from lack of oxygen.

q: A patient's heart rate is 75 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 70 mL per beat. What is the cardiac output in liters per minute? (Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.)
e: Cardiac output = 75 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 5,250 mL/min.
Convert to liters: 5,250 mL ÷ 1,000 = 5.25 L/min.
A normal resting adult cardiac output is about 5 L/min, so this answer is reasonable.

mx.5250: That's in mL/min. Divide by 1,000 to get L/min.
mx.145: Cardiac output multiplies heart rate × stroke volume; don't add.

q: Which blood type is considered the universal donor for red blood cells?
e: Type O negative red blood cells have no A, B, or Rh (D) antigens on their surface.
With no antigens to react to, they can be given to nearly any recipient in an emergency.
AB positive is the universal recipient, the opposite idea.
t: O = zerO antigens → universal dOnor.

q: A patient has type A blood. Which antibodies are normally present in this patient's plasma?
e: Type A red blood cells carry A antigens.
The plasma contains antibodies against the antigen the person does NOT have, so type A blood has anti-B antibodies.
If this patient received type B blood, the anti-B antibodies would attack the donor cells.
t: You make antibodies against the blood type you are NOT.

q: Which statements about arteries are correct? Select all that apply.
o: They carry blood away from the heart.
They have thicker muscular walls than veins.
They contain one-way valves along their length.
They carry blood at higher pressure than veins.
e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so they have thick, muscular, elastic walls.
Not all arteries carry oxygen-rich blood: the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
Valves along the vessel are a feature of veins, not arteries.

q: What is the name of the double-layered sac that surrounds the heart?
e: The pericardium encloses the heart; fluid between its layers reduces friction as the heart beats.
The pleura surrounds the lungs, the peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity, and the myocardium is the heart muscle itself.

q: The first heart sound ("lub") is caused by which event?
o: Closing of the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves
Closing of the tricuspid and mitral (AV) valves
e: When the ventricles begin to contract, pressure rises and snaps the AV valves shut, producing "lub."
"Dub" is the second sound, when the semilunar valves close as the ventricles relax.
Valve opening is normally silent.

q: In adults, where are red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets produced?
e: Hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) in adults takes place in red bone marrow, found in bones such as the hip bones, sternum, and vertebrae.
The spleen removes old red blood cells, the liver makes plasma proteins, and lymph nodes house lymphocytes but do not make all blood cells.
w: They house and train lymphocytes but don't make all blood cells.

q: The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and intestines directly to which organ?
e: After a meal, absorbed nutrients travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver before reaching the rest of the body.
This lets the liver process nutrients, store glucose as glycogen, and detoxify drugs and toxins first.

q: Put these structures in the order inhaled air passes through them, starting at the nose.
e: Air enters the nasal cavity, where it is warmed, moistened, and filtered.
It passes through the pharynx (throat) and larynx (voice box) into the trachea.
The trachea splits into the right and left primary bronchi, one to each lung.
t: "Nasty Pharaohs Like Tall Bronzes": Nasal, Pharynx, Larynx, Trachea, Bronchi.

q: Put these airways in order from largest to smallest as air moves deeper into the lung.
e: The trachea branches into primary bronchi, which branch into secondary (lobar) bronchi, one per lobe.
Bronchi keep branching into tiny bronchioles, which end in clusters of alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

q: Which muscle does most of the work during quiet breathing?
e: The diaphragm is the primary muscle of inspiration; the external intercostals help.
Abdominal muscles assist only with forced exhalation, and the pectoralis major and trapezius move the arm and shoulder.

q: Gas exchange between the lungs and the blood takes place in tiny air sacs called ______.
e: The alveoli are thin-walled sacs surrounded by capillaries.
Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

mx.bronchioles: Bronchioles carry air to the alveoli; the gas exchange happens in the alveoli.
mx.capillaries: Capillaries surround the air sacs; the sacs themselves are the alveoli.

q: Which change occurs during normal inspiration (inhalation)?
o: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity
Air pressure inside the lungs rises above the atmospheric pressure outside
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity
The external intercostal muscles relax, and the ribs move downward and inward
e: When the diaphragm contracts it moves downward, and the external intercostals lift the ribs, so the chest cavity gets bigger.
Bigger volume means lower pressure in the lungs (Boyle's law), so air flows in from the higher-pressure atmosphere.
The other choices describe exhalation.
t: Inhale: muscles contract → volume up → pressure down → air rushes in.

q: Which structure folds over the opening of the larynx during swallowing to keep food out of the airway?
e: The epiglottis is a flap of elastic cartilage that covers the laryngeal opening (glottis) when you swallow.
The uvula and soft palate close off the nasal cavity, not the larynx.
t: The epiglottis is the airway's "lid" during swallowing.

q: A baby born at 28 weeks of gestation struggles to keep the alveoli from collapsing after each breath. A deficiency of which substance is most likely the cause?
e: Surfactant is made by type II alveolar cells and lowers surface tension inside the alveoli.
Without enough surfactant, alveoli collapse at the end of each exhalation, making breathing exhausting.
The lungs do not make enough surfactant until late in pregnancy, so premature infants are at risk.
t: Surfactant works like soap in water: it lowers surface tension so alveoli don't stick shut.

q: Oxygen moves from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillary blood by which process?
o: Active transport by ATP-powered membrane pumps
Filtration driven by capillary blood pressure
Diffusion down its partial pressure gradient
e: Alveolar air has a higher partial pressure of oxygen than the blood arriving at the lungs.
Oxygen therefore diffuses down its gradient across the thin respiratory membrane; no ATP is needed.
Osmosis refers to the movement of water, not gases.

q: In a healthy person, which change is the strongest chemical stimulus to increase the rate and depth of breathing?
o: A small drop in blood oxygen level
A rise in blood glucose level
A rise in blood carbon dioxide level
A drop in core body temperature
e: Chemoreceptors in the medulla and in the carotid and aortic bodies are most sensitive to CO₂ and the H⁺ (lower pH) it forms.
Even a small rise in CO₂ quickly increases ventilation.
Oxygen must fall quite low before it becomes the main drive in a healthy person.
t: Your urge to breathe is driven mostly by CO₂, not O₂: holding your breath is ended by CO₂ build-up.

q: Which part of the brain contains the main centers that set the basic rhythm of breathing?
e: Respiratory centers in the brainstem, especially the medulla oblongata (with help from the pons), set the breathing rhythm.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, the occipital lobe processes vision, and the thalamus relays sensory information.

q: How is most of the carbon dioxide carried in the blood from the tissues to the lungs?
o: Bound to the iron atoms in hemoglobin
As dissolved carbon dioxide gas in plasma
Attached to the surface of platelets
e: About 70% of CO₂ reacts with water inside red blood cells (sped up by carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which becomes H⁺ and HCO₃⁻.
The bicarbonate moves into the plasma and is carried to the lungs.
Smaller amounts travel bound to hemoglobin's protein part (not the iron, where O₂ binds) or dissolved as gas.

q: Which structure is known as the "voice box" because it contains the vocal cords?
e: The larynx sits on top of the trachea and contains the vocal folds, which vibrate to produce sound.
The pharynx is the throat; the trachea is the windpipe.
t: Pharynx is the passage for food and air, the Larynx is for Language (speech).

q: The right lung has three lobes, but the left lung has only two. What is the best explanation?
o: The liver sits directly beneath the left lung and compresses it
The left primary bronchus is wider and shorter than the right one
The heart takes up space on the left side of the thoracic cavity
The left lung does not take part in gas exchange with the blood
e: The heart tilts toward the left, so the left lung is smaller and has an indentation called the cardiac notch.
The liver lies under the RIGHT side of the diaphragm, and both lungs exchange gases.
In fact, the right primary bronchus is the wider, more vertical one.

q: Smoking damages the ciliated cells that line the trachea and bronchi. Which function is most directly impaired?
o: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar walls
Sweeping mucus and trapped particles out of the airways
Producing surfactant to keep the alveoli open
Contracting the diaphragm during each inhalation
e: The airways are lined with cells whose cilia beat to push mucus (and trapped dust and microbes) up toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
When cilia are damaged, mucus builds up, causing "smoker's cough" and more infections.

q: During an asthma attack, which change is the main reason air flow is reduced?
o: Bronchiole smooth muscle contracts, narrowing the airways
The alveoli fill with blood and stop exchanging gases
The diaphragm becomes paralyzed and cannot contract
The cartilage rings of the trachea soften and collapse
e: Asthma involves inflammation and spasm of the smooth muscle in bronchiole walls (bronchoconstriction), plus extra mucus.
Narrower airways increase resistance, causing wheezing and difficulty exhaling.
Rescue inhalers work by relaxing this smooth muscle (bronchodilation).

q: A longtime smoker from Merced is diagnosed with emphysema, in which the walls between alveoli are destroyed. Why does this reduce oxygen uptake?
o: The airways become lined with extra cilia that block airflow
The blood loses its ability to carry carbon dioxide
The alveoli make so much surfactant that they stick shut
Less surface area is available for gas exchange
e: Breaking down the walls between alveoli merges many small sacs into fewer large ones.
Fewer, larger sacs have much less total surface area, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood.
The lungs also lose elastic recoil, so air gets trapped and exhaling is difficult.

q: Which structure is a shared passageway for both food and air?
e: The pharynx (throat) carries air to the larynx and food to the esophagus.
The larynx and trachea carry only air, and the esophagus carries only food.
t: Pharynx = shared hallway; the airway (larynx) is in front, the food tube (esophagus) is behind.

q: Tidal volume is best defined as
o: the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a deep breath
the volume of air moved in or out in one normal, quiet breath
the air that remains in the lungs after a forced exhalation
the number of breaths a person takes per minute at rest
e: Tidal volume is the normal resting breath, about 500 mL in an adult.
The maximum exhaled after a maximum inhale is vital capacity, the air left over is residual volume, and breaths per minute is respiratory rate.

q: Which are functions of the nasal cavity? Select all that apply.
o: Trapping dust and microbes in mucus
e: The nasal cavity's mucous membrane and rich blood supply warm and moisten air, and hairs and mucus filter it.
Gas exchange happens only in the alveoli, and surfactant is made by alveolar cells.

q: A student having a panic attack breathes very rapidly and deeply (hyperventilates). What happens to the blood?
o: CO₂ decreases and pH rises (more basic)
CO₂ increases and pH falls (more acidic)
CO₂ decreases and pH falls (more acidic)
CO₂ increases and pH rises (more basic)
e: Hyperventilation exhales CO₂ faster than the body makes it, so blood CO₂ falls.
Less CO₂ means less carbonic acid and fewer H⁺ ions, so pH rises: respiratory alkalosis.
This can cause dizziness and tingling in the fingers and lips.
t: CO₂ acts like an acid in the blood: blow it off and the blood becomes more basic.

q: What is the main function of the pleural fluid between the two pleural membranes?
o: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood
Reducing friction as the lungs expand and recoil
e: The visceral and parietal pleurae are separated by a thin film of serous fluid.
The fluid lets the lungs glide smoothly against the chest wall and also helps the membranes cling together so the lungs follow the chest wall as it expands.

q: Which events occur during normal, quiet exhalation? Select all that apply.
o: The diaphragm relaxes and moves upward
The volume of the thoracic cavity decreases
Air pressure in the lungs rises slightly above atmospheric pressure
e: Quiet exhalation is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, and the elastic lungs recoil.
Thoracic volume shrinks, so lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air flows out.
Contracting the external intercostals is part of inhalation, and forceful abdominal contraction happens only in forced exhalation (like coughing).

q: Put these organs in the order food passes through them, from first to last.
e: Food is chewed in the mouth, swallowed through the pharynx and esophagus, and churned in the stomach.
Most digestion and absorption finish in the small intestine, and the large intestine absorbs water and forms feces.

q: Put these regions of the intestines in the order that food residue passes through them.
e: The small intestine runs duodenum → jejunum → ileum ("Dow Jones Industrial").
The ileum empties through the ileocecal valve into the cecum, the first part of the large intestine.
From the cecum, material moves up the ascending colon, then across the transverse colon and down the descending colon.
t: Small intestine order: Dow Jones Industrial = Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum.

q: In which organ does most absorption of nutrients take place?
e: The small intestine is long and has a huge surface area, so it absorbs most nutrients.
The stomach absorbs only a few substances (such as alcohol), and the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

q: What is the main purpose of the villi and microvilli that line the small intestine?
o: To produce bile for fat digestion
To push food along the tract by peristalsis
To store food in the intestine until it is digested
To increase the surface area for absorption
e: Villi are finger-like folds, and microvilli are tiny projections on each absorptive cell (the "brush border").
Together they multiply the surface area, so more nutrients can be absorbed.
Peristalsis is done by smooth muscle layers, and bile is made by the liver.

q: Which statement about bile is correct?
o: It is produced by the gallbladder and stored in the liver
It is produced by the pancreas and stored in the gallbladder
It is produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder
It is produced by the stomach and stored in the duodenum
e: Liver cells (hepatocytes) make bile continuously.
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, then releases it into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.

q: What is the main role of bile in digestion?
o: Breaking down proteins into amino acids
Neutralizing the stomach's acid in the stomach itself
e: Bile salts break large fat globules into tiny droplets (emulsification), the way dish soap breaks up grease.
This gives lipase much more surface area to work on.
Bile has no digestive enzymes of its own.
t: Bile is the body's dish soap: it breaks up grease but does not digest it.

q: Chemical digestion of starch (carbohydrate) begins in which location?
e: Salivary glands release amylase, which starts breaking starch into smaller sugars while you chew.
Pepsin digests protein, and lipase digests fat.
Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in the small intestine.

q: Chemical digestion of protein begins in which organ?
e: Chief cells in the stomach release pepsinogen, which hydrochloric acid converts into the active enzyme pepsin.
Pepsin begins breaking proteins into smaller peptides; pancreatic enzymes finish the job in the small intestine.

q: Which enzyme breaks down dietary fats (triglycerides)?
e: "Lip-" refers to lipids (fats), so lipase digests fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides.
Amylase digests starch, pepsin digests protein, and lactase digests the milk sugar lactose.
t: Enzyme names often hint at their target: lipASE → lipids, lactASE → lactose, proteASE → proteins.

q: Peristalsis is best described as
o: the chemical breakdown of food by digestive enzymes
wavelike smooth muscle contractions that move food along
the absorption of nutrients through the intestinal wall
chewing and grinding food into smaller pieces
e: Rings of smooth muscle contract behind a food mass and relax ahead of it, squeezing it forward.
Peristalsis moves food down the esophagus and through the stomach and intestines; it does not chemically digest food.

q: What is the main function of the large intestine?
o: Absorbing water and electrolytes and forming feces
Producing bile and most digestive enzymes
Absorbing most of the nutrients from digested food
Beginning the chemical digestion of protein
e: By the time material reaches the large intestine, most nutrients have already been absorbed.
The large intestine reabsorbs much of the remaining water and electrolytes, compacting the residue into feces.
This is why problems that speed material through the colon cause watery diarrhea.

q: A patient had her gallbladder removed (cholecystectomy). Which type of meal is she most likely to have trouble digesting comfortably?
o: A meal high in lean protein
e: The gallbladder stores concentrated bile and releases a large amount when fatty food enters the duodenum.
Without it, bile trickles in continuously from the liver, so there may not be enough at once to emulsify a large fatty meal.
Starch and protein digestion depend mainly on enzymes, not bile.

q: Bacteria living in the large intestine produce a vitamin needed to make blood clotting factors. A patient on long-term antibiotics may become deficient in which vitamin?
e: Normal gut bacteria in the colon synthesize vitamin K, which the liver uses to make several clotting factors.
Long antibiotic courses can kill these bacteria, lowering vitamin K and increasing bleeding risk.
Vitamin D is made in the skin with sunlight, not by gut bacteria.
t: K is for "Koagulation" (the German spelling of coagulation).

q: A patient has frequent heartburn because stomach acid flows back into the esophagus (GERD). Weakness of which structure is most likely responsible?
e: The lower esophageal sphincter at the stomach's entrance normally keeps acidic stomach contents out of the esophagus.
The pyloric sphincter is at the stomach's exit, and the ileocecal valve and anal sphincter are much farther down the tract.

q: Which structure controls the passage of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum?
e: The pyloric sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the bottom (pylorus) of the stomach.
It releases small amounts of chyme at a time so the duodenum is not overwhelmed.
t: Pylorus = "gatekeeper" in Greek, the gate between stomach and duodenum.

q: Which is a function of the hydrochloric acid (HCl) secreted in the stomach?
o: It emulsifies dietary fats into droplets so lipase can digest them
It activates pepsin and kills many swallowed microbes
e: HCl makes the stomach very acidic (pH about 2).
This acid converts inactive pepsinogen into pepsin and destroys many bacteria in food.
Bile emulsifies fat, and amylase digests starch.

q: Which of the following are functions of the liver? Select all that apply.
o: Absorbing most nutrients from digested food
e: The liver makes bile, breaks down drugs, alcohol, and toxins, and stores glucose as glycogen (it also makes plasma proteins like albumin).
Insulin is secreted by beta cells of the pancreas, and most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

q: The semi-liquid mixture of partly digested food and gastric juice that leaves the stomach is called ______.
e: The stomach churns food with gastric juice into a soupy mixture called chyme.
Chyme passes through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum. (Do not confuse it with chyle, the fatty lymph in lacteals.)

mx.bolus: A bolus is the ball of chewed food that goes down the esophagus. After the stomach, it's chyme.
mx.chyle: Chyle is fatty lymph from the intestine. The stomach mixture is chyme.

q: Pancreatic juice contains bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). What is its main role?
o: Activating pepsin so it can digest proteins in the stomach
Neutralizing acidic chyme as it enters the duodenum
Killing bacteria in the large intestine
e: Chyme leaving the stomach is very acidic.
Bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes it, protecting the intestinal lining and providing the near-neutral pH that pancreatic enzymes need.

q: Which of the following are accessory digestive organs, meaning food does NOT pass through them? Select all that apply.
e: Accessory organs help digestion by making or storing secretions (bile, enzymes) that flow into the GI tract through ducts.
The stomach and esophagus are part of the alimentary canal (GI tract) itself, so food passes through them.
t: If food touches it, it's the GI tract; if it only sends juices in, it's an accessory organ.

q: A patient's skin and the whites of the eyes appear yellow (jaundice) because of a buildup of bilirubin. Which organ is most likely involved?
e: Bilirubin comes from the breakdown of old red blood cells and is normally processed by the liver and excreted in bile.
Liver disease (such as hepatitis or cirrhosis) or a blocked bile duct lets bilirubin build up in the blood, turning tissues yellow.

q: Carbohydrates must be digested into which form before they can be absorbed by the small intestine?
e: Only single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose, fructose, and galactose) can be absorbed.
Brush-border enzymes such as sucrase and lactase split disaccharides into monosaccharides first.
Amino acids come from protein, and fatty acids come from fat.

q: What is the basic functional cell of the nervous system that transmits electrical signals?
e: Neurons generate and conduct electrical impulses.
Glial cells support and protect neurons, a nephron is the kidney's functional unit, and an osteocyte is a bone cell.

q: Put these parts in the order a signal travels through a neuron, from where it is received to where it is passed on to the next cell.
e: Dendrites receive incoming signals and pass them to the cell body.
The impulse travels down the axon to the axon terminals, which release neurotransmitter onto the next cell.
t: Signals travel D-C-A-T: Dendrite, Cell body, Axon, Terminal.

q: A nurse taps a patient's patellar tendon and the leg kicks. Put the parts of this reflex arc in order.
o: Integration center in the spinal cord
e: A stretch receptor detects the stimulus and a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord.
The signal is processed in the spinal cord (for the knee-jerk, the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron).
A motor neuron carries the command to the effector, the quadriceps, which contracts.
t: Reflex arc: Receptor → Sensory → Integration → Motor → Effector ("Real Smart Interns Make Errors").

q: What is the main function of the myelin sheath that wraps many axons?
o: It increases the speed of nerve impulse conduction
It produces neurotransmitters for the synapse
It receives incoming signals from other neurons
It stores calcium ions needed for muscle contraction
e: Myelin is a fatty insulating layer formed by Schwann cells (PNS) and oligodendrocytes (CNS).
Impulses jump from one gap in the myelin (node of Ranvier) to the next, which is much faster than in unmyelinated axons.
In multiple sclerosis, loss of CNS myelin slows or blocks signals.

q: A patient with damage to the cerebellum would most likely have trouble with which function?
e: The cerebellum compares intended movements with actual movements and fine-tunes them, so damage causes clumsy, unsteady movements.
Language is handled mainly in the cerebral cortex, temperature by the hypothalamus, and vision by the occipital lobe.
t: Cerebellum = "little brain" for balance; think of a field sobriety test.

q: During a summer heat wave in Fresno, which brain region detects the rising body temperature and triggers sweating?
e: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat; it also regulates hunger, thirst, and the pituitary gland.
When blood temperature rises, it signals sweat glands to secrete and skin blood vessels to dilate.

q: A stroke damaging the occipital lobe of the cerebrum would most likely affect which function?
e: The occipital lobe at the back of the brain contains the primary visual cortex.
Hearing is processed in the temporal lobe, and balance relies on the cerebellum and inner ear.
t: Occipital = Optic (vision); Temporal = near the ears (hearing).

q: Which response is caused by the sympathetic ("fight-or-flight") division of the autonomic nervous system?
o: Pupils dilate and heart rate increases
Digestion speeds up and salivation increases
Pupils constrict and heart rate slows
e: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for emergencies: faster heart rate, dilated pupils and bronchioles, and more glucose released into the blood.
Digestion, salivation, pupil constriction, and bladder emptying are "rest-and-digest" parasympathetic responses.
t: Sympathetic = Stress (fight or flight); Parasympathetic = Peaceful (rest and digest).

q: Which of the following are effects of the parasympathetic nervous system? Select all that apply.
e: The parasympathetic division ("rest and digest") slows the heart, increases digestive activity, and constricts the pupils.
Dilating the bronchioles and raising blood glucose are sympathetic (fight-or-flight) effects.

q: Which of the following are part of the peripheral nervous system (PNS)? Select all that apply.
o: Ganglia (clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS)
e: The CNS is the brain (including the cerebellum) and the spinal cord.
Everything outside them, including cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia, belongs to the PNS.

q: During depolarization of a neuron's membrane in an action potential, which ion movement occurs?
o: Potassium ions (K⁺) rush into the cell
Chloride ions (Cl⁻) rush out of the cell
Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) are pumped out of the cell
Sodium ions (Na⁺) rush into the cell
e: When voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ flows into the cell, making the inside more positive (depolarization).
Repolarization follows when K⁺ channels open and K⁺ flows OUT of the cell.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump later restores the resting ion distribution.
t: Sodium In to depolarize, potassium Out to repolarize.

q: Which neurotransmitter is released by motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate skeletal muscle?
e: Motor neurons release acetylcholine (ACh), which binds receptors on the muscle fiber and triggers an action potential.
Dopamine and serotonin act mainly in the brain, and insulin is a hormone, not a neurotransmitter.

q: Which layer of the eye contains the light-sensitive photoreceptor cells?
e: The retina at the back of the eye contains rods and cones that convert light into nerve signals.
The cornea bends incoming light, the iris controls pupil size, and the sclera is the tough white outer coat.
t: The retina works like the film (or sensor) in a camera.

q: Which photoreceptors are responsible for color vision and sharp detail in bright light?
e: Cones work best in bright light and come in types sensitive to different wavelengths, allowing color vision.
Rods are more sensitive in dim light but see only shades of gray.
Hair cells are receptors in the inner ear.
t: Cones = Color; Rods = Really dim light.

q: Put these structures in the order that sound vibrations travel through them on the way to the brain.
o: Cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve
e: Sound waves travel down the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum.
The three ossicles of the middle ear amplify the vibration and pass it to the oval window.
Fluid waves in the cochlea bend hair cells, which trigger signals in the cochlear nerve to the brain.

q: A patient reports severe dizziness and a spinning sensation when turning her head. Which inner-ear structures detect rotation of the head?
e: The three semicircular canals are filled with fluid that moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells that signal the brain.
The cochlea is for hearing, the ossicles transmit sound, and the Eustachian tube equalizes middle-ear pressure.

q: Which structure of the eye changes shape to focus light on the retina for near or distant objects?
e: Ciliary muscles adjust the curvature of the lens (accommodation) to focus images on the retina.
The iris and pupil control how much light enters, and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

q: Which colored, muscular part of the eye controls the size of the pupil?
e: The iris contains smooth muscle that constricts or dilates the pupil to control how much light enters.
The pupil is the opening; the iris is the colored ring around it.

q: The narrow region between the axon terminal of one neuron and the next cell, across which neurotransmitters diffuse, is called the synaptic ______.
e: A synapse is the junction between a neuron and another cell.
The narrow space within the synapse is the synaptic cleft; neurotransmitter diffuses across it and binds receptors on the next cell.

mx.vesicle: Vesicles hold the neurotransmitter. The gap between cells is the synaptic cleft.
mx.junction: Close, but the name of the narrow gap is the synaptic cleft.

q: A patient has a stroke that damages the motor cortex in the LEFT cerebral hemisphere. Where would muscle weakness most likely appear?
o: On the right side of the body
On the left side of the body
On both sides of the body equally
Only in the muscles of the eyes
e: Most motor pathways cross to the opposite side (decussate) in the brainstem.
So the left hemisphere controls voluntary movement on the right side of the body, and vice versa.
t: Brain-to-body control is contralateral: the opposite side.

q: What is a main function of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?
o: Carrying oxygen to the bones of the skull
Transmitting nerve impulses between neurons at synapses
Cushioning and protecting the brain and spinal cord
e: CSF fills the ventricles of the brain and the space around the brain and spinal cord.
It acts as a shock absorber, makes the brain buoyant, and carries nutrients and wastes.
A lumbar puncture (spinal tap) collects CSF to test for infections such as meningitis.

q: Which neurons carry information from sensory receptors TOWARD the central nervous system?
e: Afferent neurons "arrive" at the CNS with sensory information.
Efferent (motor) neurons "exit" the CNS to muscles and glands, and interneurons connect neurons within the CNS.
Schwann cells are glial cells, not neurons.
t: Afferent = Arrive; Efferent = Exit.

q: How many bones are in the typical adult human skeleton?
e: The adult skeleton has 206 bones.
Newborns have about 270 bony parts, but many fuse together (for example, in the skull and sacrum) during growth.

q: Which type of muscle tissue is striated AND involuntary?
e: Cardiac muscle has striations (stripes) like skeletal muscle but is controlled involuntarily.
Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.
t: Cardiac muscle is the "hybrid": striped like skeletal, automatic like smooth.

q: Smooth muscle is found mainly in which location?
o: The walls of hollow organs, such as the stomach
Attached to bones of the skeleton by tendons
Only in the walls of the heart chambers
In the tongue and the muscles of facial expression
e: Smooth muscle lines hollow organs: the GI tract, blood vessels, bladder, uterus, and airways.
Skeletal muscle attaches to bones (and forms the tongue and facial muscles), and cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.

q: A soccer player at Fresno State twists her ankle and is told she has a sprain. Which structure is injured?
e: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; ligaments connect bone to bone at a joint.
A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon (tendons connect muscle to bone), and a fracture is a broken bone.
t: Ligaments link bone to bone; Tendons tie muscle to bone. SPRAIN = ligament, sTRain = Tendon/muscle.

q: Put these events of skeletal muscle contraction in order, from first to last.
o: A motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
An action potential spreads along the muscle fiber membrane
Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges
Thin filaments slide toward the center of the sarcomere
e: Acetylcholine binds receptors on the muscle fiber, starting an action potential that travels along the membrane and into the T-tubules.
This signals the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca²⁺, which binds troponin and moves tropomyosin off actin's binding sites.
Myosin heads attach to actin and pull (power stroke), sliding thin filaments inward and shortening the sarcomere.

q: During skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to which protein, allowing myosin to reach the binding sites on actin?
e: At rest, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.
Calcium binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin out of the way so cross-bridges can form.

q: After death, muscles become stiff (rigor mortis). What is the best explanation?
o: Without calcium, actin and myosin cannot bind
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Acetylcholine is released continuously after death
The bones lose calcium and lock the joints in place
e: Myosin needs a fresh molecule of ATP to release from actin after each power stroke.
After death, ATP production stops, so cross-bridges stay locked and muscles stiffen.
Calcium actually leaks into the cytoplasm after death, which allows binding; it does not prevent it.

q: The thick filaments in a sarcomere are made mainly of which protein?
e: Thick filaments are myosin, whose heads form cross-bridges.
Thin filaments are mainly actin (with troponin and tropomyosin).
Keratin is in skin and hair, and collagen is in connective tissues.

q: Which bone cells break down bone tissue, releasing calcium into the blood?
e: Osteoclasts dissolve (resorb) bone matrix.
Osteoblasts build new bone, osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix, and chondrocytes are cartilage cells.
t: Osteo-CLASTS = Cut (break down); Osteo-BLASTS = Build.

q: Which of the following are characteristics of skeletal muscle tissue? Select all that apply.
o: Found in the walls of blood vessels
e: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated, striated cells that we control voluntarily.
Smooth muscle lines blood vessel walls, and intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells.

q: Which bone is part of the axial skeleton?
e: The axial skeleton forms the body's central axis: skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum.
The femur (limb), scapula, and clavicle (pectoral girdle) belong to the appendicular skeleton.
t: Axial = along the body's axis (skull, spine, ribs, sternum); appendicular = appendages and the girdles that attach them.

q: Which type of joint allows the widest range of motion, including rotation in many directions?
o: Hinge joint, such as the elbow
Ball-and-socket joint, such as the shoulder
Pivot joint, such as between the first two vertebrae
Suture, such as between skull bones
e: In a ball-and-socket joint, the rounded head of one bone fits into a cup of another, allowing movement in all planes.
Hinge joints move in one plane, pivot joints allow rotation around one axis, and sutures are essentially immovable.

q: The sutures that join the bones of an adult skull are classified as
e: Sutures are fibrous joints in which bones are bound by dense connective tissue and essentially do not move (synarthroses).
Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and move freely; cartilaginous joints like the intervertebral discs move slightly.

q: An older woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis after a hip fracture. Which imbalance best describes what has been happening in her bones?
o: Bone building by osteoblasts has exceeded bone breakdown by osteoclasts
Cartilage has gradually replaced compact bone
Red bone marrow has replaced all of the yellow marrow
Bone breakdown by osteoclasts has exceeded bone building by osteoblasts
e: Bone is constantly remodeled; in osteoporosis, resorption outpaces formation, so bones lose mass and become porous and fragile.
After menopause, falling estrogen allows osteoclast activity to increase, which is why older women are at higher risk.
Weight-bearing exercise, calcium, and vitamin D help maintain bone density.

q: Bending the elbow so the hand moves toward the shoulder is an example of which movement?
e: Flexion decreases the angle between two bones at a joint.
Straightening the elbow is extension, abduction moves a limb away from the midline, and rotation turns a bone around its own axis.

q: Raising your arm out to the side, away from the midline of the body, is called
e: Abduction moves a body part away from the midline (think "abducted" = taken away).
Adduction brings it back toward the midline (you "add" it back to the body).
Supination turns the palm to face up or forward.

q: Which vitamin is needed for the intestine to absorb calcium, supporting healthy bones?
e: Active vitamin D (calcitriol) increases calcium absorption from the small intestine.
Without enough vitamin D, bones become soft (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults).
Vitamin C is needed for collagen, but it does not control calcium absorption.

q: Which of the following are functions of the skeletal system? Select all that apply.
o: Supporting the body and protecting internal organs
Producing blood cells in red bone marrow
Producing most of the body's heat
e: Bones support and protect (the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs), store minerals, and house red marrow that makes blood cells.
Most body heat comes from contracting skeletal MUSCLE, and digestive enzymes come from digestive glands.

q: Bone-forming cells that secrete new bone matrix are called ______.
e: Osteoblasts build bone by laying down collagen and helping it mineralize.
Once surrounded by matrix, an osteoblast becomes an osteocyte.

mx.osteoclasts: Osteoclasts break down (Clear away) bone. Osteoblasts Build it.
mx.osteoclast: Osteoclasts break down (Clear away) bone. Osteoblasts Build it.
mx.osteocytes: Osteocytes are mature bone cells trapped in matrix. The builders are osteoblasts.

q: When the biceps brachii contracts to flex the elbow, the triceps brachii relaxes. In this movement, the triceps is acting as the
e: The prime mover (here the biceps) is mainly responsible for the movement.
The antagonist (the triceps) opposes that movement and must relax for it to happen; it is the prime mover for elbow extension.

q: The diaphragm is made of which type of muscle tissue?
e: The diaphragm is a skeletal muscle controlled by the phrenic nerves.
Breathing usually happens automatically, but you can also control it voluntarily (holding your breath), which fits skeletal muscle.
t: Automatic does not always mean smooth muscle: if you can override it on purpose, think skeletal.

q: Osteoarthritis, common in older adults, mainly involves the wearing away of which tissue?
o: Articular cartilage covering the ends of bones
The periosteum covering the shaft of the bone
The tendons and skeletal muscles that cross the joint
e: In synovial joints, smooth hyaline (articular) cartilage covers the bone ends and reduces friction.
In osteoarthritis this cartilage breaks down, so bone rubs on bone, causing pain and stiffness.

q: Which of the following is part of the body's first line of defense against pathogens?
o: Cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells
e: The first line of defense consists of physical and chemical barriers that keep pathogens out: skin, mucous membranes, tears, stomach acid.
Fever and inflammation are part of the second (internal innate) line, and antibodies and T cells are the adaptive third line.

q: Which of the following are part of innate (nonspecific) immunity? Select all that apply.
e: Innate defenses respond quickly and the same way to many different invaders: inflammation, fever, and phagocytes such as neutrophils.
Antibodies from plasma cells and memory T cells are adaptive: they target specific antigens and remember them.
t: Innate = born with it, fast, general. Adaptive = learned, slower the first time, specific, has memory.

q: Which cells produce and secrete antibodies?
e: When a B cell is activated by its specific antigen, it multiplies and many of its offspring become plasma cells.
Plasma cells are antibody factories; helper T cells help activate B cells but do not make antibodies.

q: HIV damages the immune system mainly by destroying which cells?
e: HIV infects and destroys CD4⁺ helper T cells.
Helper T cells coordinate both antibody and cell-mediated responses, so losing them weakens the whole adaptive immune system and leads to opportunistic infections.

q: Which cells directly kill body cells that are infected with a virus?
e: Cytotoxic (CD8⁺) T cells recognize viral antigens displayed on infected cells and release chemicals that kill those cells.
Helper T cells coordinate the response, B cells make antibodies (via plasma cells), and basophils release histamine.
t: Cytotoxic = "cell poison": these T cells are the immune system's assassins.

q: Which white blood cells are the most abundant in blood and usually the first to arrive at a site of bacterial infection?
e: Neutrophils make up about 50–70% of white blood cells and quickly leave the blood to phagocytize bacteria.
A high neutrophil count often signals a bacterial infection.
Pus is largely made of dead neutrophils.
t: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas: Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils.

q: Which of the following are classic signs of inflammation at an injured site? Select all that apply.
e: Inflammation dilates local blood vessels (redness and heat) and makes them leakier (swelling).
Swelling and chemicals released by damaged cells cause pain.
The area becomes red, not pale, because more blood flows to it.
t: Four cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor = redness, heat, swelling, pain.

q: A nursing student receives the hepatitis B vaccine before starting clinicals. Which type of immunity does this produce?
e: A vaccine exposes the body to antigens, so the student's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells: active immunity.
Because it comes from a medical intervention instead of a natural infection, it is artificially acquired.

q: A newborn receives antibodies from the mother through breast milk. Which type of immunity is this?
e: The infant receives ready-made antibodies rather than making its own, so the immunity is passive (and temporary, with no memory cells).
It happens through a normal process (nursing or transfer across the placenta), so it is naturally acquired.
t: Active = your body does the work. Passive = someone hands you antibodies.

q: A child who had chickenpox is exposed to the virus again years later and does not get sick. What best explains this?
o: Memory B and T cells mount a faster, stronger secondary response
The virus can no longer infect skin cells
The first infection destroyed all the body's receptors for the virus
e: During the first infection, some activated lymphocytes became long-lived memory cells.
On re-exposure, memory cells respond quickly and produce large amounts of antibody, usually before symptoms develop.
This immunological memory is the basis for how vaccines work.

q: During a throat infection, the lymph nodes in the neck become swollen and tender. Why?
o: The nodes are producing extra red blood cells
Bile is backing up into the lymph vessels
The nodes are storing excess dietary fat
Lymphocytes in the nodes are multiplying
e: Lymph nodes filter lymph and are packed with lymphocytes and macrophages.
When they encounter antigens from the infection, lymphocytes multiply rapidly, enlarging the nodes.

q: Besides immune defense, what is a major function of the lymphatic system?
o: Pumping blood from the heart to the lungs
Producing digestive enzymes for the intestine
Returning excess tissue fluid to the blood
Filtering urea out of the blood into urine
e: Some fluid leaks out of capillaries and is not reabsorbed; lymphatic vessels collect this fluid (lymph) and return it to veins near the heart.
If lymph vessels are blocked or removed (for example, after some cancer surgeries), fluid builds up and causes swelling (lymphedema).
Lymphatic vessels in the intestine (lacteals) also absorb dietary fats.

q: Put the steps of phagocytosis by a macrophage in order.
o: The phagocyte recognizes and attaches to the microbe
The phagocyte engulfs the microbe, enclosing it in a phagosome
A lysosome fuses with the phagosome
e: The phagocyte first binds the microbe (antibodies or complement coating it make this easier).
It wraps its membrane around the microbe, forming a vesicle called a phagosome.
A lysosome fuses with it, and digestive enzymes destroy the microbe.

q: In which organ do T lymphocytes mature?
e: T cells form in red bone marrow, then travel to the thymus (T for thymus) to mature.
The thymus is largest in childhood and shrinks with age.
The thyroid is an endocrine gland, not a lymphatic organ.
t: B cells mature in Bone marrow; T cells mature in the Thymus.

q: Which organ filters blood, removes old and damaged red blood cells, and is located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen?
e: The spleen filters blood, breaks down worn-out red blood cells, and contains lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne pathogens.
The liver is mainly in the right upper quadrant, and the thymus is in the chest.

q: The Y-shaped proteins made by plasma cells that bind to specific antigens are called ______.
e: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) bind specific antigens.
Binding can neutralize toxins, clump microbes together, and mark them for destruction by phagocytes.

mx.antigens: Antigens are the targets. The Y-shaped proteins that bind them are antibodies.
mx.antigen: Antigens are the targets. The Y-shaped proteins that bind them are antibodies.

q: An antigen is best defined as
o: a Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells
a type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests bacteria
a chemical released by the brain to cause fever
a molecule that triggers a specific immune response
e: Antigens are usually proteins or large carbohydrates (on microbes, pollen, or transplanted cells) that trigger an immune response.
Antibodies are the proteins made to bind antigens; do not mix up the two.
t: ANTIGEN = ANTIbody GENerator.

q: During an allergic reaction to almond pollen, mast cells release a chemical that dilates blood vessels and causes itching and a runny nose. Which chemical is this?
e: Mast cells (and basophils) release histamine, which dilates blood vessels and makes them leaky.
This causes redness, swelling, itching, and mucus, which is why antihistamines relieve allergy symptoms.
t: Anti-HISTAMINE drugs block histamine, the main allergy messenger.

q: A patient develops sudden airway swelling, wheezing, and a dangerous drop in blood pressure minutes after a bee sting (anaphylaxis). Which medication is given first to reverse these effects?
e: Anaphylaxis is a whole-body allergic reaction with massive histamine release.
Epinephrine constricts blood vessels (raising blood pressure) and relaxes bronchiole smooth muscle (opening airways), which is why it is given right away by auto-injector.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do nothing for an allergic reaction.

q: Which lymphatic tissues, located in the walls of the pharynx, trap pathogens that are inhaled or swallowed?
e: The tonsils are clusters of lymphatic tissue around the throat that sample and fight microbes entering through the mouth and nose.
Inflamed tonsils (tonsillitis) are a common sign of a throat infection.
The thymus is in the chest, the spleen is in the abdomen, and the inguinal lymph nodes are in the groin.

q: Which of the following is an autoimmune disease, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues?
e: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas.
Influenza (virus), strep throat (bacterium), and Valley fever (a fungus common in Central Valley soil) are infections caused by outside pathogens.

q: Macrophages, the large phagocytes found in tissues, develop from which type of white blood cell?
e: Monocytes circulate in the blood, then leave it and enlarge into macrophages in the tissues.
Macrophages engulf microbes and debris and present antigens to T cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

q: Insulin is produced by which cells?
o: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
e: The pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) contain beta cells, which secrete insulin, and alpha cells, which secrete glucagon.
The liver responds to insulin, but it does not make it.
t: Beta cells → Bring blood sugar down (insulin). Alpha cells → glucAgon raises it.

q: Name the hormone that lowers blood glucose by helping glucose enter body cells.
e: After a meal, rising blood glucose stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin.
Insulin helps glucose enter muscle and fat cells and signals the liver to store glucose as glycogen.

mx.glucagon: Glucagon RAISES blood glucose. Insulin lowers it.
mx.glycogen: Glycogen is stored glucose, not a hormone.

q: Between meals, blood glucose begins to drop. Which hormone is released to raise it, and how does it work?
o: Insulin; it signals the liver and muscles to store glucose as glycogen
Glucagon; it signals muscle cells to absorb more glucose from the blood
Calcitonin; it releases glucose from bone
Glucagon; it signals the liver to break down glycogen into glucose
e: Pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon when blood glucose falls.
Glucagon tells the liver to break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
Insulin has the opposite effect, lowering blood glucose.
t: Glucagon = "glucose is gone," so release more.

q: A patient with type 2 diabetes has high blood glucose even though the pancreas is still producing insulin. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The immune system has destroyed all of the beta cells
The liver has completely stopped making glucagon
Body cells have become resistant to insulin's effects
The kidneys are secreting too much insulin into the blood
e: In type 2 diabetes, cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance), so glucose stays in the blood.
Destruction of beta cells by the immune system describes type 1 diabetes.
The kidneys do not produce insulin.

q: Which structure releases hormones that directly control secretion by the anterior pituitary gland?
e: The hypothalamus releases releasing and inhibiting hormones that travel through a portal system to the anterior pituitary.
Because it controls the pituitary, the hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.
t: The hypothalamus is the boss of the pituitary, which is the boss of many other glands.

q: A farmworker in Fresno County is becoming dehydrated during a 108 °F afternoon. Which hormone increases to help the kidneys conserve water?
e: When blood becomes more concentrated, the hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release ADH.
ADH makes the kidney's collecting ducts reabsorb more water, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine.
(Aldosterone also helps by retaining sodium, but it was not offered as a choice.)
t: Anti-DIURETIC = against making lots of urine.

q: A patient with hyperthyroidism (too much thyroid hormone) would most likely show which set of signs?
o: Weight gain, slow heart rate, and cold intolerance
Low blood calcium, muscle cramps, and spasms
Very high blood glucose and frequent urination only
Weight loss, rapid heart rate, and heat intolerance
e: Thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄) raise the body's metabolic rate.
Too much speeds everything up: weight loss despite eating, fast heart rate, nervousness, and feeling hot.
Weight gain, a slow heart rate, and feeling cold describe HYPOthyroidism.
t: HYPER-thyroid = everything speeds up; HYPO-thyroid = everything slows down.

q: Which mineral must be supplied in the diet for the thyroid gland to make its hormones T₃ and T₄?
e: T₃ and T₄ contain iodine atoms (the numbers refer to how many each has).
A lack of dietary iodine can cause an enlarged thyroid (goiter); iodized salt prevents this.

q: Blood calcium is too low. Which hormone is released, and from which gland, to raise it?
o: Calcitonin, from the thyroid gland in the neck
e: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, increasing calcium reabsorption by the kidneys, and activating vitamin D.
Calcitonin from the thyroid has the opposite effect and lowers blood calcium.
t: PTH Pulls calcium out of bone; calciTONin TONes it down.

q: Blood levels of thyroid hormone (T₃ and T₄) rise above normal. Through negative feedback, what happens next?
o: The thyroid gland releases even more T₃ and T₄
The adrenal medulla releases more TSH
e: High T₃ and T₄ inhibit the hypothalamus (TRH) and anterior pituitary (TSH).
Less TSH means less stimulation of the thyroid, so hormone levels fall back toward normal.
TSH comes from the anterior pituitary, not the adrenal medulla.

q: Put these steps of thyroid hormone regulation in order.
o: The anterior pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
The thyroid gland releases T₃ and T₄
Body cells increase their metabolic rate
e: TRH from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH.
TSH travels in the blood to the thyroid, which releases T₃ and T₄.
These hormones raise cellular metabolism, and high levels feed back to slow TRH and TSH release.

q: Which gland secretes epinephrine (adrenaline) during a sudden fight-or-flight emergency?
e: The adrenal medulla, the inner part of each adrenal gland, is stimulated by sympathetic nerves to release epinephrine and norepinephrine.
The adrenal cortex (outer part) makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone.
t: Medulla = middle (inner) part; cortex = outer "bark."

q: Aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex, causes the kidneys to
o: excrete more sodium and more water into the urine
reabsorb sodium (and water) and excrete potassium
e: Aldosterone acts on the distal tubules and collecting ducts to reabsorb Na⁺ and secrete K⁺.
Water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and blood pressure increase.
t: Where sodium goes, water follows.

q: Which hormone is released by the adrenal cortex during long-term stress and raises blood glucose while suppressing inflammation?
e: Cortisol, a glucocorticoid, raises blood glucose by promoting glucose formation and breakdown of stored fuels.
It also suppresses inflammation and the immune response, which is why cortisol-like drugs (such as prednisone) are used for inflammatory conditions.
Epinephrine is the short-term stress hormone from the adrenal medulla.

q: Which gland secretes melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle?
e: The pineal gland, deep in the brain, releases melatonin mainly in darkness, helping make you sleepy at night.

q: Which hormones are produced and secreted by the anterior pituitary gland? Select all that apply.
e: The anterior pituitary makes GH, TSH, prolactin, ACTH, FSH, and LH.
Oxytocin (and ADH) are made in the hypothalamus and released from the POSTERIOR pituitary.
Insulin comes from beta cells of the pancreas.

q: After childbirth, which hormone stimulates the mammary glands to PRODUCE milk?
e: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production.
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causes milk ejection ("let-down") from the ducts, not production.
t: PROlactin PROduces milk; oxytocin moves it Out.

q: How do endocrine glands deliver their hormones to target cells?
o: They release hormones through ducts onto the skin
They empty hormones into the digestive tract
They secrete hormones into the bloodstream
They pass hormones directly along nerve axons
e: Endocrine glands are ductless; their hormones diffuse into nearby capillaries and travel in the blood.
Exocrine glands (sweat, salivary) use ducts to release secretions onto a surface or into a cavity.

q: Which of the following are endocrine glands? Select all that apply.
e: The thyroid, adrenal glands, and pituitary secrete hormones directly into the blood.
Salivary and sweat glands are exocrine glands; they release their products through ducts.
t: Endocrine = into the blood (ductless); Exocrine = exits through a duct.

q: Steroid hormones such as cortisol and estrogen bind to receptors located inside target cells. Why can they reach these receptors?
o: They are pumped in by sodium–potassium pumps
They are lipid-soluble and cross the plasma membrane
They are large proteins that enter through channels
They are carried into cells attached to red blood cells
e: Steroid hormones are made from cholesterol, so they are lipid-soluble.
They pass through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, often changing gene expression.
Water-soluble protein hormones such as insulin cannot cross the membrane; they bind receptors on the cell surface.

q: A hormone travels in the blood to every part of the body, yet it affects only certain cells. Why?
o: Only its target cells have receptors for that hormone
The hormone is destroyed in all other tissues first
Only target cells are reached by the blood supply
The hormone can only travel in one direction
e: A cell can respond to a hormone only if it has the matching receptor.
Cells without the receptor are exposed to the hormone but do not respond.

q: Which organ produces most of the testosterone in males?
e: Interstitial (Leydig) cells in the testes produce testosterone, under the control of LH from the anterior pituitary.
The prostate makes part of the seminal fluid but does not produce testosterone.

q: Put these organs in the order urine passes through them, from where it is formed to where it leaves the body.
e: Urine forms in the kidneys and flows down the ureters to the urinary bladder, where it is stored.
It leaves the body through the urethra.
t: Ureter comes before urethra: alphabetically "ureTEr" leads to the bladder, "ureTHra" goes to THe outside.

q: Put these parts of the nephron in the order that filtrate flows through them.
e: Blood is filtered at the glomerulus, and filtrate enters the glomerular capsule.
Filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop, and the distal convoluted tubule.
Several nephrons drain into a collecting duct, where final water reabsorption is adjusted by ADH.

q: What is the functional unit of the kidney, where urine is formed?
e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons, each of which filters blood and processes the filtrate into urine.
The glomerulus is only the filtering part of the nephron; neurons and alveoli belong to other systems.

q: In which part of the nephron does filtration of blood plasma take place?
e: Blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the glomerular capsule.
Blood cells and large proteins are normally too big to be filtered.
The tubules and collecting duct handle reabsorption and secretion.

q: Most reabsorption of water, glucose, amino acids, and sodium from the filtrate occurs in which part of the nephron?
e: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered water and sodium and normally all of the glucose and amino acids.
Its cells have microvilli that increase surface area for this work.
The collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption, and the bladder only stores urine.
w: This is where blood is filtered, not where most is reabsorbed.
These only carry and store urine.

q: Which of the following is normally NOT found in the urine of a healthy person?
e: Blood cells are too large to pass through a healthy glomerular filter, so red blood cells in urine (hematuria) suggest disease, injury, or infection.
Urea, water, and sodium ions are normal components of urine.

q: A routine urinalysis shows glucose in a patient's urine. Which condition is this most often associated with?
e: Normally, all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
When blood glucose is very high, the filtrate contains more glucose than the transporters can reabsorb, so glucose spills into the urine (glycosuria).
This is why untreated diabetes causes frequent urination and thirst.

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease often develops anemia. Which hormone, normally made by the kidneys, is most likely deficient?
e: The kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO) when blood oxygen is low; EPO stimulates red bone marrow to make red blood cells.
Damaged kidneys make less EPO, so fewer red blood cells are made.
Renin is also made by the kidneys, but it regulates blood pressure, not red blood cell production.
t: Kidneys make EPO: "Erythro" = red, "poiesis" = making.

q: Urea, the main nitrogen-containing waste in urine, is produced from the breakdown of
e: When amino acids are broken down, their nitrogen-containing amino groups form toxic ammonia.
The liver converts ammonia into less toxic urea, which the kidneys excrete.
Fats and carbohydrates contain no nitrogen, so they do not produce urea.

q: Urinary tract infections are more common in females than in males. What is the main anatomical reason?
o: The female bladder is lined with skin
The female urethra is much shorter
e: The female urethra is only about 4 cm long and opens close to the anus, so bacteria can reach the bladder more easily.
The male urethra is about 20 cm long, which makes it harder for bacteria to travel up it.

q: How do the kidneys help correct blood that has become too acidic?
o: By excreting bicarbonate and reabsorbing H⁺ ions
By excreting H⁺ ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate
By releasing extra carbon dioxide gas into the urine
e: The kidneys secrete hydrogen ions into the urine and return bicarbonate (a base) to the blood.
Both actions raise blood pH back toward the normal range of about 7.35–7.45.
The lungs, not the kidneys, adjust CO₂.

q: Drinking alcohol inhibits the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). What is the expected effect on urine?
o: A larger volume of more dilute urine
A smaller volume of more concentrated urine
e: ADH normally tells the collecting ducts to reabsorb water.
With less ADH, less water is reabsorbed, so more water stays in the urine: more urine, and more dilute.
This water loss is one reason alcohol contributes to dehydration.
t: Less ADH → more urine; more ADH → less urine.

q: In which structure does fertilization of an egg by a sperm normally occur?
e: After ovulation, the egg is swept into the uterine tube, where it is usually fertilized.
The resulting embryo travels to the uterus over several days and implants in the uterine lining.
t: Fertilization in the tube, implantation in the uterus.

q: In a healthy person, which substances are normally reabsorbed from the kidney filtrate back into the blood? Select all that apply.
e: Most filtered water and essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Creatinine, a muscle waste product, is not reabsorbed and is excreted in urine.
Excess H⁺ ions are secreted INTO the filtrate to help control blood pH, not reabsorbed.

q: Put these structures in the order sperm pass through them, from production to exit.
e: Sperm form in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis.
During ejaculation they travel through the ductus deferens and ejaculatory duct into the urethra.
A vasectomy cuts the ductus deferens, so sperm can no longer reach the urethra.

q: Which event directly triggers ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovary?
o: A sudden drop in estrogen levels
A sharp rise in prolactin levels
A surge of insulin from the pancreas
e: As a follicle matures, rising estrogen triggers a sharp LH surge from the anterior pituitary.
The LH surge causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the egg, about midway through the cycle.
Home ovulation tests detect this LH surge.

q: In a normal pregnancy, the embryo implants in which layer of the uterus?
e: The endometrium is the inner, blood-rich lining that thickens each cycle to receive an embryo.
The myometrium is the thick smooth-muscle layer that contracts during labor, and the perimetrium is the outer covering.

q: Home pregnancy tests detect which hormone in urine?
e: Soon after implantation, the developing placenta secretes hCG.
hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, which maintains the uterine lining in early pregnancy.
t: hCG = the "I'm pregnant" hormone made by the developing placenta.

q: If pregnancy does not occur, menstruation begins about two weeks after ovulation. What directly causes the uterine lining to shed?
o: A surge of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary
Estrogen levels rise sharply in the bloodstream
The ovary releases a second egg into the uterine tube
Progesterone falls as the corpus luteum breaks down
e: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and estrogen), which maintains the thickened endometrium.
Without hCG from a pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone drops.
Without progesterone support, the endometrium breaks down and is shed as menstrual flow.

q: Which of the following are functions of the kidneys? Select all that apply.
o: Helping regulate blood pressure by releasing renin
Storing urine until it is released
e: The kidneys filter blood, help control blood pressure (renin), and release erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production.
The urinary bladder stores urine, and the liver produces bile.

q: The tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body is the ______.
e: The urethra drains the bladder to the outside.
Do not confuse it with the ureter, which carries urine from a kidney to the bladder (there are two ureters but only one urethra).

mx.ureter: The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. From the bladder out is the urethra.
mx.ureters: The ureters carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. From the bladder out is the urethra.

q: An older man has trouble starting urination and a weak urine stream. Enlargement of which gland, which surrounds the urethra just below the bladder, is the most likely cause?
e: The prostate wraps around the first part of the male urethra.
When it enlarges with age (benign prostatic hyperplasia), it squeezes the urethra and obstructs urine flow.

q: What is the outermost layer of the skin?
e: The epidermis is the thin, outer layer of stratified squamous epithelium.
The dermis lies beneath it, and the hypodermis lies beneath the dermis. The periosteum covers bone.
t: EPI = upon: the epidermis sits upon the dermis.

q: A nurse gives an intramuscular injection in the upper arm. Put these layers in the order the needle passes through them, from the surface inward.
e: The needle passes through the epidermis and then the dermis, which contains blood vessels and nerves.
Next is the fatty hypodermis (where subcutaneous injections such as insulin are given), and finally the deltoid muscle.

q: Put the layers (strata) of the epidermis of thick skin, such as the palm, in order from the surface to the deepest layer.
e: The deepest layer, the stratum basale, contains dividing stem cells.
As cells are pushed upward through the spinosum and granulosum, they fill with keratin and die.
Thick skin has an extra clear layer, the lucidum, under the outermost layer of dead, flat cells, the stratum corneum.
t: From surface to deep: "Come, Let's Get Sun Burned" (Corneum, Lucidum, Granulosum, Spinosum, Basale).

q: Compared with lightly pigmented skin, darkly pigmented skin typically has
o: many more melanocytes spread through every layer of the epidermis
similar numbers of melanocytes that make more melanin
melanocytes located in the dermis instead of the epidermis
a much thicker dermis that blocks ultraviolet light
e: People of all skin tones have roughly similar numbers of melanocytes in the stratum basale.
Differences in skin color come mainly from how much and what type of melanin those melanocytes make and pass to keratinocytes.

q: Which cells make up most of the epidermis and produce the tough protein that waterproofs and protects the skin?
e: Keratinocytes are about 90% of epidermal cells and produce keratin.
